utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor against Dusko Tadic, case No. IT-94-1-PT.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, Judge Karibi-Whyte has granted the Prosecutor's motion for leave to file an amended indictment in this matter. ((Repeated for technical reasons) Pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, Judge Karibi-Whyte granted the request of the Prosecutor for leave to file an amended indictment. This morning the Chamber will receive from the accused an entry of a plea to that amended indictment. We will also today hear from counsel regarding their readiness for trial and, perhaps, request that the Registrar set a date for the trial. After we complete that matter, we will consider in open court two motions that have been filed by the Defence; first, a motion as to the form of the indictment and, secondly, a motion on non bis in idem. Thereafter, we will hear in a closed session the Prosecutor's motion for protective measures with respect to witness L. As I indicated, that motion will be heard in a closed session. The Prosecutor has requested that it be heard in a closed session and that is unopposed by the Defence. Am I correct, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we will be very busy this morning and, perhaps, into the afternoon. May I have the appearances, please, for counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is my Niemann. I appear with my colleagues to my right, Miss Hollis, to my left, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Keegan and Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I have two short applications before the initial appearance on the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For the Defence, may I have appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, on my right side, for you on my left side, is Mr. Andre Klip who is an expert consultant assisting the Defence; next to me, Mr. Alphons Orie, co-counsel in this case, and on my left side, for you on your right side, is Mr. Vujin; my name is Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic has previously filed an affidavit of indigency requesting the assignment of counsel pursuant to Rule 45 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. The Registrar has appointed at the request of Mr. Tadic Mr. Michail Wladimiroff to proceed as lead counsel in this matter. Mr. Vujin has appeared on several occasions to assist Mr. Wladimiroff. I see that Mr. Orie is here today. Mr. Orie, you have been present on more than one occasion as we have proceeded. Mr. Simic, who has often appeared with Mr. Vujin, is not present today. Are you ready to proceed with the entry of a plea to the amended indictment, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, should we proceed with the entry of a plea before you handle this preliminary matter which I am not sure exactly what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would probably be preferable if I raised these two short matters now before the plea is entered. The first is an application under Rule 50. I have discussed this with my colleague, Mr. Wladimiroff, and by consent we seek to amend count 5 of the amended indictment. There is a reference in count 5 in relation to the violation of the laws or customs of war description. There is a reference there to Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. That reads: "Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) and 7(1) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949." If your Honours please, the 7(1) is misplaced there; it should appear after "Article 3" as it first appears in count 5. We have asked that it be amended so that "Article 7(1)" is moved to the position immediately after "Article 3" where it appears.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then it would be Article 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, so it should read that way.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Rule 50 provides that the Prosecutor may amend an indictment without leave at any time before its confirmation, but thereafter only with the leave of the Judge who confirmed it or, if at trial, with leave of the Trial Chamber. We will interpret that Rule to mean that this request is an amendment made at trial and we will act on it. There is unanimity on that point, so that trial amendment will be granted with respect to count 5 of the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my second application (and again this is by consent and after discussion with my colleague, Mr. Wladimiroff) relates to the reference in the indictment to the accused Goran Borovnica. In respect of that accused we would make an application by consent under Rule 82(B) for an order that there be separate trials, that the trial of Borovnica take place at some other time to this trial that is presently proceeding in relation to the accused Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Rule provides: "The Trial Chamber may order that persons accused jointly under Rule 48 be tried separately if it considers it is necessary in order to avoid a conflict of interests that might cause serious prejudice to an accused, or to protect the interests of justice".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our application is, if your Honours please, based on that part of the provision that relates to protect the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any opposition to that request, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then that request will also be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am not quite sure what you are doing here. As I understand it, Borovnica is not accused at all. There is no count against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would say that count 11 does accuse him. Admittedly ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Do you mean count 11 or paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: There is no count under paragraph 11 in respect of him, is there? If he suddenly appeared, he could not be convicted under this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be, your Honour, that the paragraph would be more elegantly expressed if it said "by participation in these acts Dusko Tadic and Goran Borovnica", but I am not sure, your Honour, that the omission of his name from that place excludes him from being tried under that count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Are you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He is mentioned, if your Honour pleases, "including Dusko Tadic and Goran Borovnica" in the leading part of the paragraph. Also, there is reference to him, if your Honours please, right up at the front of the indictment in the introduction part where he is specifically referred to in paragraph 1, in particular, in the last three lines: "The accused Goran Borovnica participated with Dusko Tadic". So there may be some ambiguity which is, no doubt, an issue which could be RAISED should a trial against Goran Borovnica take place but, in our submission, your Honour, the indictment does, in fact, accuse him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I suppose for the present accused it does not really matter, but it just seems curious that we do not have any allegation of Borovnica committing any offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I agree, your Honour, that it would have been better if his name had been included after Dusko Tadic and before the word "committed". I would submit that it is not fatal but again it is not an issue that needs determining now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it seems, your Honour, should there be any doubt about an issue of whether or not it is perceived that a trial against Goran Borovnica is now proceeding because he is mentioned in the indictment, for the sake of appearances, if nothing else, it is, in our submission, in the interests of justice that a formal order be made that there be separate trials.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that is the concern that we have that we have addressed previously, that is, to make it very clear that this trial will not be proceeding against this accused who is absent. I gather Mr. Wladimiroff is not representing this accused, so any deficiencies that there are in this amended indictment will, I suppose, have to be addressed at a later time should you intend to proceed under this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But so far as this accused is concerned, this second accused will be severed and there will be a separate trial, if and when the Prosecutor is ready. Is that how you wish to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is our application.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Then that request is granted as well. That is unopposed by counsel for Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Anything else preliminarily, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. With those preliminary matters out of the way, Mr. Wladimiroff, are you ready to proceed with the entry of a plea to the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you ready for Mr. Tadic to enter a plea with respect to the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We are, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, has Mr. Tadic received a copy of the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has he received a copy of the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He did, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has Mr. Tadic read the amended indictment or has he had it read to him in a language that he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He has got a translation of the indictment in his own language.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your opinion, does Mr. Tadic understand the nature of the charges that are made in the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have been discussing the nature of the charges and I take it that he understands the nature of it in the context as we discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that he understands the nature of the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There may be some doubt but, in general, he understands what the type of allegations it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He understands to a sufficient extent to proceed with the entry of a plea at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. I think that Mr. Tadic is attempting to have you turn to him. If you wish an opportunity to confer with Mr. Tadic at this time, you may have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I want to enter my plea, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I want to enter my plea concerning the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Wladimiroff, does Mr. Tadic wish to have the amended indictment read in its entirety or is he willing to waive the reading of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He is willing to waive the reading of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you please rise? Would you please stand up, Mr. Tadic? For the record, would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My name is Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you ready to enter a plea?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, are you ready to enter a plea to the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I am, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You understand that the amended indictment will not be read in its entirety at this time and you will be entering a plea to it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I have read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Tadic, how do you plead to the amended indictment, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have read the indictment, and I have talked to my lawyers about it. I do not understand the indictment and, judging by everything I have seen in it, what I managed to understand, concerning that I can say that I have not participated in any one of the mentioned crimes. I was not present when any one of the crimes mentioned in the indictment were committed. I have said that I do not understand the indictment, not because it was not translated -- it has been translated -- but I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you understand the nature of the charges that are made against you? I understand what you say when you say that you were not present when these alleged acts occurred; do you understand what charge is being made in the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I do not fully understand the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you need additional time to speak with Mr. Tadic? Perhaps he is not understanding what I mean when I ask him does he understand. Of course, he is not a lawyer but he has to rely on you and if he understands the nature of the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think I should enlighten you on this issue. In my assessment of the situation, Mr. Tadic understands the facts as related in the indictment. What he is saying to you is that he was not related to any of these facts. He does not understand the legal nature of the charges, and that is what he is trying to tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you have heard what Mr. Wladimiroff has said; is that a correct statement of your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With that understanding, Mr. Wladimiroff, do you believe that Mr. Tadic is ready to proceed then with the entry of a plea to the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then the court will accept the entry of a plea of not guilty to the amended indictment in its entirety. Thank you. Mr. Tadic, you may be seated. You may sit down, Mr. Tadic, thank you. As I indicated, the next task, so to speak, on our agenda today will be to enquire of the parties as to their readiness for trial. Mr. Niemann, is the Prosecutor ready to proceed to trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is ready to proceed, your Honour, for trial, if your Honour pleas.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Wladimiroff, is the Defence to ready to proceed to trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We are ready to proceed with the hearing of the motions. We are not ready to proceed for a trial. If you want me to explain that, I will enlighten you on that problem too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would appreciate it. Yesterday we had a conference with the lawyers and Mr. Tadic was present. The purpose of our conference was to discuss preliminarily certain matters that may relate to the scheduling of the trial as well as how the trial would be conducted. I think it is important for that matter to be discussed. As I recall, the Prosecutor had indicated that it was ready to proceed with trial. You wished 30 days notice, as I recall, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, for a date to be set, we would appreciate 30 days, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you had expressed the difficulties that you are encountering that affect your readiness to proceed. I would appreciate your telling the Chamber about those difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. I will, your Honour. I do regret that the Defence is not ready to proceed, that is, that we are not able to start with the trial in the time of, let us say, one month, as is the wish of the Prosecution. As a matter of fact, we are far from ready to start with the trial because we have been investigating the amended indictment up to 9th September when I was in the area of the Opstina of Prijedor and Banja Luka when I had to leave the area because of the NATO bombing. After that it has not been possible for me to enter the area again. It is a war zone nowadays and, therefore, it is not possible for me to go into the area. For that same reason Mr. Simic is not here at the hearings; he cannot leave the area. Even if I was able to enter into the area to locate witnesses and to interview witnesses, I have experience that I have no co-operation whatsoever of the local authorities. On the contrary, I have experienced that people in any official capacity, such as policemen and military men, are ordered not to speak with me. So we are terribly handicapped and, therefore, not able to conclude the investigations on the initial indictment. We fear that from the moment that we will be able to enter the area again, the problems as I indicated with the local authorities will not have been changed, though Mr. Vujin is doing what he can to achieve a better position. We have to wait what will happen. But even so, if the authorities will co-operate, I am afraid just because I have been informed that a lot of people are displaced, are no longer living there, so we have to locate them again and that will take substantial time, as I fear. Further, I have been assigned by the Tribunal just myself to Mr. Tadic. I have to litigate the case and I have to investigate the case. I cannot do both at the same time. I have been assisted on a voluntary basis by the gentleman sitting here on the bench with me, but that is just incidental, not on a daily basis. So I feel also very handicapped because I am not adequately funded by the Tribunal to defend Mr. Tadic as I should do. I fear that when I will be able to enter the area again, and if the authorities will be co-operative, and if I have located the witnesses I am looking for, that will take me a substantial time to do the job just by myself. In the meantime, it will be very difficult for me to litigate the case. So what I am trying to say is that I am far from ready for the initial indictment. I have not even been able to start to investigate the amended indictment, because the amended indictment was released in September and at that time I was in Yugoslavia. When I had to come back, I had no opportunity to go into that matter. So the Defence is not ready to proceed for the trial. We feel that if the trial would start now or within a month or even this year, that would certainly not be a fair trial because we are not able to present any witness except for some we have investigated related to the initial indictment. What we ask, and we have asked that to the Registry -- we will repeat it here again -- we are only able to proceed and to try to conclude our work within a reasonable time if we are well funded and able to have a team working on this matter. For that reason we have asked for a researcher to investigate, as a co-counsel who can work on the case on a daily basis and a possibility to retain expert consultants. The problem is that all these kinds of costs have not been foreseen in the budget of the Tribunal. So, as I understand the Registry is under negotiation with the authorities to arrange for a better funding, but we fear that if these negotiations continue it will be too late. So we urge the Tribunal (and maybe I should file just by now an oral motion) that a continuation of the trial under these conditions will be a mistrial. We take the position that continuation of the trial without a proper funding of the Defence, without a proper opportunity for the Defence to prepare the case, would not be a fair trial for Mr. Tadic. We think that if we are well funded and able to enter the area again, and if we assume that it will be possible somewhere in March or February, if I am optimistic -- that has also something to do with the weather circumstances -- we think we are able to proceed with the trial somewhere in May. Once again I express my regret that we have no other way to deal with the problem as I just explained to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, we have, as I indicated -- "we" meaning the Trial Chamber -- met, I think, two times with counsel during which we have discussed this question of remuneration of counsel. I do believe that the Chamber, at least, has expressed sympathy at the very least with the position that you find yourself in. The Tribunal does have guidelines for the appointment of counsel. In those guidelines, of course, there are amounts that are set out. Those guidelines were established very early after we began the process of developing rules. The guidelines, I suppose, I do not recall exactly but it seems to me that you had suggested in our conversation that, whatever the hourly rate was or daily rate, it amounted to $26 per hour or guilders, is it? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: $26 per hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if you divided then this $200 American by the number of hours, I thought, 7.5, we come to whatever the maths shows. So we, of course, were concerned and, of course, the guidelines do not call for the appointment of co-counsel or investigators, paralegals or an expert witness. But I do understand that the Registrar's office has worked with you, or attempted to work with you, to meet some of those requests for your travels, at least, to the former Yugoslavia. So, of course, when you accepted the assignment you were aware of these guidelines, but we are all embarking on rather unchartered waters. We have all found that things are not what they seemed, perhaps, when we began this process. So we, at least, as a Chamber, believe that it is imperative for consideration to be made of certainly some of your requests. I want you to understand that we are sympathetic to it. After we met yesterday I took a look at what we have been doing, I suppose, since the initial appearance. I found that all of us were pretty busy. Mr. Tadic was indicted in February. We had to wait from February, I suppose, until sometime in April for German legislation to be passed that would enable Germany to transfer Mr. Tadic to the Tribunal because he was in custody there. We then had our initial appearance in April. We then met again in June and had the hearings on additional motions. We met again in July and had hearings on additional motions. On August 10th this Trial Chamber issued its decision on jurisdiction as well as the protective measures motion. There then was an appeal and the Appeals Chamber had its hearing and then issued a decision on October 2nd. So you have been very busy since you began this representation and we are very much aware of that. The Prosecution has been very busy too. So we can only hope that some consideration is given to your request. As I understand it, the Registry has been in communication with the United Nations. This is not my responsibility -- as Judges, we are not really involved in this -- but there is an amount in the budget at least that has been approved by the General Assembly that, perhaps, would enable some flexibility and some modification of the guidelines of appointment of counsel to meet some of the concerns that you have raised. So, although the amount is in the budget, though, the question is whether it can be spent. I am not really that much involved with the Registrar, but she is certainly making a sincere effort to meet your concerns. We only hope, as a Tribunal, that even though there are these financial difficulties that we hear about -- as a matter of fact, just this morning I saw something on the news about the financial difficulties of the UN; we are certainly aware of that -- we certainly hope that in terms of the setting of priorities with respect to the expenditure, that in the setting of priorities that recognition will be given to the mandate that this Tribunal has and this mandate was to proceed with trials. They knew, the Security Council knew, that when we were created there was an ongoing conflict, that the conflict was thousands of miles away. The Tribunal does not have a police force, so there is no way that we can enforce or request. We have to rely on the co-operation of states. So, there are all of these difficulties that are inherent in the creation of the Tribunal. When the General Assembly approved the budget in July of this year, I would imagine that they were aware of these. So, I only hope that being aware of the difficulties that we operate in and being aware in advance, that when we were established there was recognition that there was a need to go forward. Hopefully, in the setting of priorities, as I say, some attention will be given, because we certainly are anxious to proceed to trial but we want to afford you an opportunity to engage in appropriate investigation, discovery, in order to afford Mr. Tadic his fair trial. We are concerned about that and that is our utmost concern. So we hope that something is forthcoming and we will be able to proceed with this matter. We did understand that you needed certain documents, that is, the accompanying documents to the amended indictment needed to be translated. I spoke with the Registrar this morning and some of those actually have been translated -- not all of them. You are perfectly correct that you need all of them translated. That will be done. I think we had yesterday talked about November 23rd. Perhaps that can be done a little more quickly; instead of four weeks, perhaps it will be two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you had indicated that you would need 30 days then to make a decision as to whether you would be asserting certain defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then that got us then to December 23rd. Then after that you indicated that you would need an additional three months to investigate. This takes going to the former Yugoslavia with an ongoing conflict. That would then get us to March 23rd, if my dates are correct. Thereafter, you had indicated you would need six weeks to prepare and that would get us to May 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right, all on the presumption that I will be permitted to enter the area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand. As I indicated, to a great extent the Tribunal is dependent upon the co-operation of states. We are simply without the police power to make those kinds of demands. So we certainly hope that that co-operation will be given so that we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The reason why I repeat the aspect is that we have to take consideration that almost all witnesses on the part of the Prosecution are living outside of the former Yugoslavia while our witnesses are living inside. So there is a difference, a quite large difference, in the position.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What the Chamber will do then is to set a another pretrial conference for January 16th 1996, at 10 a.m. From what we have heard today, it looks like the trial may possibly begin on May 6th. So we will tentatively set that as our date, but when we meet on January 16th we will want to assess what progress has been made and, perhaps, resolve any matters that are impeding (to the extent that we can) your progress towards preparation for trial; perhaps on January 16th set a firm date for trial, but tentatively we are thinking that trial may commence on May 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise a matter? We are, of course, very sympathetic to the issues that Mr. Wladimiroff has raised. We are concerned, however, that circumstances change from time to time which, perhaps, may facilitate Mr. Wladimiroff moving the matter forward a little faster. One of the ideas that occurred to us, if we could have on a regular basis, about every six weeks, perhaps, say, a pretrial conference or status conference just to see how matters are proceeding. We would find that a better way of proceeding in terms of trying to get closer to trial. We are just concerned about too long delays between these conferences. As your Honour has mentioned 16th January, that may be a sufficient period, but I thought perhaps if there was an opportunity between now and the end of year to have another short conference -- I am not talking about something lengthy, but just a short conference -- where we can just see how things are progressing, we, the Prosecution, would feel much more comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We, of course, are available at the pleasure, so to speak, of counsel for the Prosecution as well as the Defence. Where we are now, however, though, is that the material is to be gotten in translated form to the Defence and that will be done no later than November 23rd. Thereafter, the Defence has indicated that it will review that material and then by December 23rd notify whether it wishes to assert any defences that are specified in our Rules. I do not know truly what the Chamber can do between that period but we, of course, are available. The reason that we said January 16th as a pretrial or status conference was because it was at that date that the parties then have exchanged the material that we think is necessary for the Defence (and the Defence has said) to go forward. So I do not think that it is really necessary, but we are available, for sure. As we indicated yesterday, we are very anxious to meet with counsel as often as possible to resolve any problems that you might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not want to press the matter too firmly, except that if a trial date is not set on 16th January, then perhaps I will renew this application that we have regular status conferences, because we are becoming concerned about a lengthy delay in the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think you are right -- I will hear from Mr. Wladimiroff -- but it probably would occur after January. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no problem in more meetings after January. Before January, the Defence intends to convert my oral admission into a written motion in December, if the funding is not resolved. So we will be here anyhow if there is a serious problem going on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Anything else? Then we will proceed, the pretrial conference will be set for January 16th at 10 a.m. Of course, if counsel have any matters that you wish to discuss with us before then, you are always free to request an informal conference or status conference with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, we will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there are no additional matters then that need to be discussed regarding the readiness for trial and the trial setting -- Mr. Niemann, let me ask you one question, though, how long do you anticipate that the trial will require? Of course, you can only speak for your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From our point of view, your Honours, we think the trial will probably run from six to eight weeks from the point of view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the time it would take for you to put on your case in chief. That does not include time for cross-examination because you cannot estimate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have attempted to include cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have, OK. Let us then proceed to, if we may, a hearing on the motion on the form of indictment. The Defence has filed a motion on the form of the indictment. The Prosecutor has responded to that motion. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, to arrange for the presentation?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, what we will do is to stand in recess, if we may, for 10 minutes. Then when we return we will proceed with the motion on the form of the indictment and then non bis in idem. (Short adjournment) (11.00 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you wish to proceed with the motion on the form of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. It seems to the Defence that the amended indictment has replaced the initial indictment since the initial indictment is incorporated in the amended indictment. If this is true, the initial indictment is no longer existing for that reason. The first motion filed by the Defence on June 23rd of this year would no longer make any sense; whereas there is no essential difference between the motion on the initial indictment and the motion on the amended indictment, nor as there is, as we see it, between both responses of the Prosecution by defer to the opinion of the Trial Chamber on the validity of the first motion. Let me confine myself to the second motion: Before going into the allegation of vagueness or multiplication, I should first address two issues, I think. The implication of the confirmation procedure of Rule 47 and the implication of Rule 62(i) where the Trial Chamber has to satisfy itself that the accused understands the indictment. In the opinion of the Defence, it follows from the system of the Rules that a confirmation of the indictment does not exclude a defence on the form of the indictment, simply because the defendant (and, of course, after confirmation, the accused) has no standing in the system of the Rules to dispute the form of the indictment during the procedure of confirmation. The accused may only arise such a defence after the initial hearing within a period of 60 days. The question now of Rule 62(i) is merely a formal one and does not implicate a waiver of any defence on the form of the indictment. On the occasion of the initial appearance of Mr. Tadic on April 26th of this year, nothing more in this context had been asked by the presiding Judge than: "Do you believe Mr. Tadic understands the nature of the charges contained in the indictment?" As a matter of fact, you asked my client today the same question related to the amended indictment. On behalf of the accused, I responded in April: "I think he understands the nature of the charges". Today, I used a more complicated formula but, anyhow, you understood what I meant; there is a difference between understanding what is in the indictment, if we read the words in the factual sense, and what is in the indictment if he tries to understand the indictment in legal terms. So, I think there is no legal problem here. The accused is fully entitled to dispute the form of the indictment. So let me now turn to the vagueness: Article 18(4) of the Statute and Rule 47(B) provides for an indictment on the basis of a charge containing a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes. The question now is, what means a concise statement of the facts and the crime? To start with, it follows from international accepted standards of human rights that in a fair administration of justice any charge of an indictment should provide for an adequate description of the alleged crime or crimes, and of the alleged culpable part of the accused in it, allowing the accused a proper preparation for his defence. The Defence, therefore, takes the position that the concise statement of facts and crime may not limit the standards and should be understood as an adequate description that enables an accused to defend himself properly. What is required for a description of a charge in an indictment to enable an accused to defend himself? I would say a unique and factual description of both the criminal offence and of the participation of the accused in that offence. So, what means unique and factual? By unique and factual description, I mean a factual description of the alleged behaviour or omission of the accused at a specific time, at a specific place, resulting in a specific crime that individualises the charged event from any other event. Only if an indictment provides for such a description the accused will know for which offence and crime he has been charged. Only in that case, it will be possible to investigate the allegations and to develop a proper defence. If an indictment does not provide for such a description, the Defence may face unmountable problems. For example, an undetailed indication of the criminal offence without any facts related to the alleged behaviour of the accused mounting up the charged crime frustrates the Defence to investigate and to address such a vague allegation. Another example, a very wide time frame and extensive location of the alleged event will almost block a defence of alibi. The Defence takes the position that the amended indictment does not provide for an adequate description, as I explained before, the amended indictment does not provide for an adequate description of the alleged crimes and of the alleged culpable part of the accused in these crimes as required in a fair administration of justice. The indictment fails to provide for a unique and factual description of the alleged behaviour of Dusko Tadic at specific times and places resulting into specific crimes that individualise each charged account from other accounts. This failure to provide for an adequate description can easily be demonstrated, for example, by paragraph 4 of the amended indictment where Dusko Tadic is charged with three crimes, count 1, persecution on political, racial and/or religious grounds; count 2, deportation and, count 3, unlawful deportation and/or transfer or unlawful confinement of a civilian. To keep things simple, I will confine myself to the example of count 1, the charge of persecution. This persecution has not been described as an individual event but as a part of other events in a very spacious time frame, in very general terms without any detail about the criminal offence of persecution itself, and without any fact related to the alleged behaviour of Dusko Tadic without a proper limitation in place of event. Let me explain this. For persecution, the relevant description of time only reads "between about 23rd of May 1992 and about 31st December 1992." This time frame of more than six months has not been narrowed to a specific moment of time in any other relevant part of the amended indictment. All we know is that the alleged persecution took place in a period of 23rd May up to 31st December 1992. I now turn to the location: For persecution, the relevant description of the location reads: "Muslim and Croat residential areas" and further it reads "camps located in Omarska, Keraterm Trnepolje", and finally we read "residents of the municipality". The general description of location under No. 1 of the amended indictment is not relevant for count 1 because this paragraph at paragraph 1 only refers to, "participation of Dusko Tadic in the attack on, seizure, murder and maltreatment of Bosnian Muslims or Croats in the Opstina of Prijedor both within the camps and outside the camps". No reference is made to persecution as charged under count 1. We now turn to the background description under paragraph 2.1 to 2.7. This paragraph only narrows the place where the persecution as charged under count 1 as allegedly happened to "The Opstina of Prijedor", to "Kozarac" and to "other places in the Opstina". If we then turn to the general allegations as described under paragraphs 3.1 up to 3.9, this paragraph does not supply any additional information about a location, place, where the persecution as charged under count 1 took place. So all we know about the location is that the alleged persecution took place in the Opstina of Prijedor, that is Kozarac and other places in the Opstina. Then, if we now focus on the question by which behaviour Dusko Tadic allegedly has committed the persecution, the description under paragraph 4 of the amended indictment only provides for a general description without any explanation of facts. It only states that Dusko Tadic has participated in all kinds of events of a legal nature, while the Defence is not sure which of the events is relevant for the alleged persecution of count 1. Let me explain this. Is it participation in "attack on residential areas", an event that has not been further elaborated in the indictment, or was it "destruction" or "plunder" in that area? The Defence does not know whether these kinds of events of illegal nature are relevant for participation in a persecution. Is it participation in the "seizure" of Muslim and/or Croats, an event that has also not been elaborated in the indictment or was it "imprisonment" or "deportation" or "expulsion"? It is not quite clear to the Defence. Is it participation in the "subjection to a campaign of terror", also not further elaborated in the indictment, or was it "killings", "rapes", "assaults" or participation in "other physical or psychological abuse"? It is not quite clear to the Defence. It is clear however, that the description of this alleged participation in all these different events does not provide for a factual description of the behaviour by Dusko Tadic mounting up to a persecution of people as charged under count 1. All we know is that the alleged persecution took place by participation in all kinds of generally indicated events of an illegal nature. So what do we know after all? So what do we know about the charge of persecution? From the indictment, we know that Dusko Tadic allegedly participated in all kinds of events, such as "attacks on residential areas", "destruction", "plunder", "seizure", "imprisonment", "deportation" and all the others I already quoted in the Opstina of Prijedor during the periods of May to December 1992. Is that a unique factual description that enables the Defence to prepare the case? We believe no, we believe not, because we do not know how Dusko Tadic allegedly participated in all these events, and which events may constitute the persecution as recognised by Article 5(h) of the Statute committed by Dusko Tadic in conformity with Article 7 of the Statute. As a matter of fact, we do not know. The indictment does not provide the necessary information of factual kinds not being unique. In the opinion of the Defence, all these issues should be addressed in the indictment itself, and not separately by supplementary material provided through discovery or by disclosure. If I now may turn to that material because I just demonstrated by count 1 what our problems are. I have abstained from demonstrating each count in the same way, but we could. Let me now turn to the material provided to the Defence by the Prosecution. That material contains a statement of fact, that is, a concise summary of all statements that have also been provided to the Defence by the Prosecution of possible witnesses of the Prosecution as being a short compilation of these statements sorted out per set of counts, not per count. We judge it as a service to the Defence, but not being a part of the indictment, certainly not a statement of fact served out per count and being additional evidence to the indictment as sufficient for a unique and factual description of each count. The statement of facts does not describe the part of Dusko Tadic in each of the events as charged. The statement of fact does not describe the specific time frame of each of the events as charged. The statement of fact does not describe the specific location where each of the charged events took place. The Defence takes the position that on the basis of the present indictment we are not able to defend Mr. Tadic properly. As a matter of fact, the Defence is faced with the burden of open-ended allegations that frustrate an effective examination of witnesses. Given the limitations of the Rules and directives allowing an indignant accused to be defended by one assigned counsel only -- I already addressed this issue -- it will not be possible to investigate in due time a defence of alibi of such an extensive period of time without proper details of facts and locations. A witness, for example, cannot be examined about a specific day or on a specific behaviour or on a specific place or location. If a witness, for example, for the Prosecution will confine himself to a date, an alibi for that date will be without any effect as long as another witness may refer to other dates within the spacious time frame. It is almost impossible to cross-examine witnesses if the time frame is so spacious. The same applies for the place of events. Any location within the Opstina of Prijedor, or within Kozarac, or within each of the camps may be sufficient to prove the indicted count. That also handicaps the Defence in cross-examination of witnesses. Under these circumstances, the Prosecution should be ordered to specify for each count the alleged behaviour of Dusko Tadic in terms of specific time, specific location and specific behaviour. The trial of Dusko Tadic should, therefore, only start when such specifications have been added to the indictment and after the Defence will have proper time to prepare. If that is not possible, all charges not being in conformity with the proper indictment that enables the Defence to defend the accused properly should be dismissed. Let me now turn to the issue of multiplication of charges. Since both parties will file a pretrial brief about the requirements of crimes to be war crimes, simply saying about the elements of the criminal provisions, I will not address any longer that aspect of the matter. It seems to me quite economical if I confine myself to the multiplication itself. Addressing that allegation, that the amended indictment contains an unreasonable multiplication of charges for the same behaviour, I think I have to exclude, first, some probable misunderstandings. First of all, the Defence has no problem with the joinder of two or more different crimes occurring as one offence at the same location if the these crimes are the result of different acts or omissions. We also do not oppose the possibility of charging a series of related acts committed by the same accused joined in a single indictment. We have no problem with that. So far so good, but when a single act committed by an accused might violate multiple criminal provisions, we do only not oppose those multiple charges may be brought in a single indictment as long as each charge of a criminal provision is an alternative to the other. What I am saying here is that the application of a criminal provision resulting from a specific act or omission should exclude the application at the same time of another criminal provision resulting from the same act or omission. Why do I say this? I am saying this because this point of view is in conformity with the system of the criminal law of the former Yugoslavia, is consistent with the present criminal law of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is consistent with the criminal law of the present Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and is consistent with the criminal law of the present Bosnian-Serb Republic. If in the system of criminal law of the former Yugoslavia one specific act of a defendant falls into different criminal provisions, only one provision may be imposed on the defendant. In this system concurrent charges are not possible, only alternative charges. In practice, the Prosecution will either choose to indict only one provision or indict each provision but as an alternative to the others, if the others are not proven. In this system, usually the provision with the highest punishment absolves the other provisions, or the specific provision will set aside an applicable general provision, Lex specialis derogat lex generalis. The alternative of this system that allows only a penalty for one criminal provision by blocking a conviction for two criminal provisions resulting from the same act, from one and the same act, is to provide for sentencing guidelines to reduce a multiplication of punishments, as seems to be the case in the United States. From this background, I think we should look now into the Statute. The crimes of Articles 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the Statute are not the product of a coherent system of prohibitions but, rather, a compilation of provisions of Conventions of different times and different origin and in many cases overlapping each other. We have learned, for example, by the Appeal Chambers that, as a matter of fact, Article 3 covers all. So what does it mean? In this compilation of customary international law condensed in the Statute, one and the same act is covered by more than one provision of Articles 2 to 5 of the Statute. The Statute and the Rules of the Tribunal do not address the possibility of this multiplication of charges. The matter raised by the Defence is, therefore, not settled, but to the discretion of the Trial Chamber to be decided in accordance with a fair trial. In determining the sentence, however, the Rules direct the Trial Chamber to take into account the general practice regarding prison sentences of the former Yugoslavia. You are instructed to do so in Article 24 and it has been elaborated in Rule 101(B) at (iii). Since in the system of criminal law of the former Yugoslavia, as I already indicated, only one provision arising from the same act may be imposed on the defendant, the general practice of prison sentences do not address the problem of multiple charges for one and the same act. So, here we face a problem, because there is no alternative which could be the case if there were sentencing guidelines. Those guidelines are not in the Yugoslav system. You are instructed to apply the general practice regarding prison sentences in the former Yugoslavia. In this situation, the Defence suggests that the Prosecutor should not be allowed to indict the accused with multiple charges for the same behaviour. That would be the easiest way to avoid confusion. If I may return to my example of the acts described paragraph 4 of the amended indictment? I draw your attention to the concurrence of deportation in count 2 and in count 3. Those counts may result from one and the same behaviour. As long as the general practice of a prison sentence of the former Yugoslavia does not address this problem of multiple charges for one and the same act, then an indictment with multiple charges for the same act is unfair to the accused. Therefore, to conclude my presentation, the Defence suggests that such an indictment should be denied to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who will present argument for the Prosecution? Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Good morning. If it pleases the court, as the Defence stated, your Honours, the standard by which this Trial Chamber must consider this indictment in the light of the Defence challenge are the requirements of the Tribunal Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Counsel for the Defence correctly cited Article 18(4) and Rule 47(B) of the Tribunal Rules which together established a requirement for a valid indictment before this Tribunal. To satisfy the requirements of the Tribunal, an indictment must contain the names and particulars of the accused and a concise statement of the facts and of the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged. The prosecution submits that the indictment in this case fully complies with the requirements of both Article 18(4) and Rule 47(B). The Defence argument regarding the form of the indictment, we submit, misconstrues the purpose of the indictment under the Statute and the Tribunal Rules. The indictment is not, nor is it intended to be, the total submission of the Prosecution to the Defence in any particular case, and is not intended to be the only source of relevant information about charges that the Defence receives from which it can determine what defences, if any, exist. The purpose of the indictment under the Statute and the Tribunal Rules can be read from Articles 20 and Rule 62. That purpose is to place the accused on notice of the nature of the charges alleged against him or her with sufficient specificity that the accused can understand the nature of the charges and be able to enter pleas to each charge. In order to provide that effective notice, the indictment must state the precise nature of the charges, that is, the legal description, for example, a violation of Article 2(B), willfully causing great suffering, and the cause of those charges, that is, the basic facts which support the charge. The statement of the cause of the charges is sufficient if the conduct of the accused described, if true, would constitute the offence alleged, and if it states an offence which is within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. This indictment certainly meets that burden. The allegation by Defence counsel regarding the nature or quantity of the information which must be in the indictment, that is, the right of the accused to receive a full description of the time, place, actions and means of each crime as a conditio sine qua non for a fair trial, is not truly an issue relevant to the sufficiency of the indictment. Rather, it goes to the rights of the accused under Article 24(A) and (B) of the Statute and Rules 66 through 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the rights of the accused to have detailed information regarding the charges against him and adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his Defence. There is no question in this case of the Defence not receiving that information which is both relevant and detailed about the crimes with which the accused is charged. As the Defence stated in its motion on the amended indictment, the Prosecution has agreed and, in fact, did turn over all supporting material for the amended indictment in advance of the time required by the Rules. Defence counsel's argument regarding the Tribunal Rules indicates not only, one, a question of whether this indictment is sufficient, but also a potential criticism of whether the Tribunal Rules and Statute are the proper standard by which this Trial Chamber should consider the matter. As stated in paragraph 106 of the Secretary General's Report: "It is axiomatic that the International Tribunal must fully respect the internationally recognised standards regarding the rights of the accused at all stages of its proceedings. In the view of the Secretary General, such internationally recognised standards are, in particular, contained in Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Paragraph 106 of the Secretary General's Report speaks in reference to Article 21 of the Statute which is entitled "Rights of the Accused". Paragraph 4(a) of that Article is derived from Article 14(3)(a) of the Covenant of Civil and Political Rights and is the basic right from which the requirements for the indictment before the Tribunal is derived. The question is, what does the language of Article 14(3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political rights mean? What does it require? In part, the relevant part of that language is that the accused has the right to be "informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him". The term "nature and cause of the charge" means, according to the comments to the Covenant, "not only the exact legal description of the offence but also the facts underlying it". The comments go on to say that the information must be sufficient to allow for the preparation of a defence pursuant to Article 14(3)(b), that is, the right mentioned earlier of the accused to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of a defence. The comments go on to state that the "information must thus be provided with the lodging of the charge or shortly thereafter, with the opening of the preliminary judicial investigation or with the setting of some other hearing that gives rise to a clear official suspicion against an accused person". As with the other provisions addressing fundamental rights in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, this commentary addresses the observation of an accused's right to detailed information regarding the crimes with which he or she is charged in general terms, and it must do so because it must account for a variety of judicial and penal systems. Thus, Article 14 of the International Covenant does not demand that the rights set forth in paragraph 3(a) be fulfilled in any specific format or by any particular document. Rather, it only requires that the accused be informed of the nature and cause of the charges against him or her, in detail, at or near the time that the accused is the subject of official charges or initial proceedings. It is clear that the Tribunal's process, as a whole, meets those requirements. The indictment is simply a part of the process and it is designed, as stated above, to place the accused on notice of the nature of the charges alleged against him or her with sufficient specificity so that the accused can understand the nature of the charges and be able to enter pleas to each charge. It seems, based on the arguments of Defence counsel, your Honour, that it is, if you will, the purpose of the indictment which is the essential issue here for the Defence. It is our submission that the indictment is not intended, when it is drafted or presented, to anticipate what defences the accused might like to allege in a particular case. The purpose of the indictment is to state the nature and basis of the crimes alleged by the Prosecutor against the accused. So, to the extent that they do not fulfil all of the wishes of Defence counsel as regards his case, is not the issue. As to the issue of the requirements of the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, we would cite Article 48, paragraph 1, copies of which have been furnished to the court and to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is Article 48 of the code?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. "Concurrence of Criminal Offences" is the title of the article. The English translation follows. In fact, in paragraph 1 it states: "If the perpetrator by one deed has committed several criminal offences or by several deeds has committed several criminal offences which are tried concurrently, the court shall first determine punishment for each criminal offence and then proceed with the pronouncement of a unified sentence." It would appear to the Office of the Prosecutor that language, on its face, makes it clear that, in fact, under the law of the former Yugoslavia, which is now the current law in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that, in fact, a conviction can stand for multiple crimes on the basis of a single course of conduct of the accused. The issue is then resolved, as you see there, by specific format for sentencing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I understand that Mr. Wladimiroff is suggesting, or it is his position, that the charges should be charged alternatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Our position -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What are you saying -- and that is the way it is done in Yugoslavia, charged alternatively, or at least I thought that was his position. Here, in your indictment, you do not charge alternatively. You charge ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, we do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- the same acts constituting a violation of different either Conventions or Articles of our Statute. Are you saying then that Article 348 recognises that there need not be a requirement to charge alternatively?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. That is the way I would read that plain language in the first paragraph. In addition, ma'am, of course, the issue of the reference to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina is an issue to sentencing upon conviction which, of course, is not the issue that is relevant to this motion, which is a question of whether or not it is sufficient on its face and then the subsequent issue of concurrence of charges. The issues of how, if there is conviction, the crimes should be considered for sentencing is best properly left to that point of the trial after a conviction. The issue here on the concurrence of charges, if it please the court, we believe, does not contain an unreasonable concurrence or multiplication of charges, nor does it expose the accused to double jeopardy. Rule 49 of the Tribunal Rules, as cited by counsel, allows for the joinder of two or more crimes in an indictment if the series of acts committed together form the same transaction, and the said crimes were committed by the same accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something? The very fact that Yugoslav Article 48 is headed "Concurrence", and in paragraph 1 talks about one deed resulting in several criminal offences, you say that shows by implication at least, although it is dealing with punishment, that an indictment or the Yugoslav equivalent can deal with one act resulting in a number of offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Not in the alternative?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One would have thought there must be an earlier Article that deals with the way in which the charges may be put so that we do not have to rely on that implication. Is the answer that it does not appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The other Article is, in fact, an Article relating to the types of verdicts, which you also have in that package, the pronouncement of verdict, which was the only Article we could find relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It would be ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 348?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Article 348, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, if I understand the Defence, they are suggesting that there are some guidelines that would tell the sentencing judge in the former Yugoslavia to do that. There are sentencing guidelines in the United States and, perhaps, other jurisdictions. We do not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So there is a possibility, I suppose, that we could then sentence on each of the counts, even though it was the same act or acts that constituted the offence, but it seems to me does not the appeal's decision give us some guidance in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe, the Rules for the Tribunal for sentencing do refer to that the Tribunal must make reference to the laws in the former Yugoslavia as to sentencing. So I believe that there would be some impact in that regard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So then what you are saying is that we would then look to Article 348 and apply the sentencing procedure utilized under that Article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe that the court would have to make reference to Article, I believe it is, 48 for sentencing, the Concurrence. However, as I said earlier, your Honour, I believe that is an issue which would be more appropriately and fully addressed at the time of sentencing, assuming there is a conviction in the case. That particular issue of how the sentencing formula would be worked out is not relevant to the issue of the indictment and whether or not multiple offences can stand in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If an error is made in sentencing, assuming there is a finding of guilt, then that is something, then there is an appeal procedure that can be dealt with ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- and there is no way for us for it to be anticipated at this point that an error is going to be made in sentencing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask something else? You are distinguishing between, as I understand it, the time of the indictment and the purpose the indictment serves and the subsequent time of immediately before the trial. You say Article 21 of the Statute and 21(4)(a), in particular, deals with the latter situation, and that is not the subject matter of this application which is concerned only with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I am saying, exactly, that the Defence is blending two issues here: One is strictly what are the technical requirements for a legally sufficient indictment; the other issue is having the information and facilities and time to mount an adequate defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: My point then, if that is as I understand you, that the Chamber does not have the necessary information. A statement of facts was referred to, that is not something before the Chamber. We do not know anything about the exchange of testimony of witnesses that are going to be called. All that goes to the question of the ability to mount a defence, I suppose. You say none of that is relevant in this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct. What is relevant here is whether or not the indictment, on its face, is sufficient under the requirements of the Statute and Rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just follow that point -- then I have a question really for Mr. Wladimiroff as it relates to this -- the first issue, it seems to me, that we need to talk about is what is the standard for a review of the indictment. What you have proposed is that the standard is whether or not the indictment informs the accused of the nature and cause of the charge against him. You say that is set out in Article 23 of our Statute and that comes from Article 14, I forget the subsection, (3) or whatever it is, of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. That is where it comes from, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Defence, however, says: "Well, the standard is to provide the accused with a unique and factual description of the crime and his participation", and he would ask for a specific time, specific place, etc. I gather that is not the standard that you would have us apply, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am, that is correct. That cite, of course, was without any particular authority.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What I was asserting was that the Secretary General's Report tells us specifically what standard or what authority they were looking to when they drafted the Statute, and from which then you developed the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That goes to Article 14 of the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights. That standard is spelled out. What it says is that the accused has the right to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands the nature and cause of the charges. My point is that the indictment is only one part of that requirement. The purpose of the indictment for this Tribunal, as in most jurisdictions, is to inform the accused of the charges on a sufficient basis to enable the accused to plead. Then there are other provisions relating to discovery, and other support for the Defence to allow for a proper defence. It is really two issues, and the Defence has blended those two issues for the purposes of their motion. That is my essential point, that we need to break away this issue of the ability to adequately prepare a defence from the particular requirements for a sufficient indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And that the International Covenant recognises that when it provides that the purpose is to inform the accused of the nature of the charges against him, and then makes reference to additional supplementary material that, of course, may at some point be made available to the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Right. It does that by in the comment saying that this information which must be provided "must be provided with the lodging of the charge or shortly thereafter, with the opening of the preliminary judicial investigation or with the setting of some other hearing that gives rise to clear, official suspicion against a specific person". The point of that is, as with most international covenants or agreements, they must be described....issues in general terms because they must account for a variety of systems, particular systems, national systems. That is exactly what the International Covenant does. It says, this basic right must be respected, but it provides a wide enough latitude to account for individual systems. Our submission is that here under our Statute and Rules, we meet that requirement through the entire process here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The process -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The indictment is only one part of that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Along with the indictment, amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You have always discovery, etc.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You provide the accused with the supporting material that accompanied the indictment, and that would include statements and other matters that you submitted to the confirming Judge; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not a discovery device; that is something that is provided to the accused after the initial appearance; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But in this instance it has been, I believe provided as it relates to the amended indictment to the accused already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that Mr. Wladimiroff says that is a convenience to the accused, and it still does not, when he looks at it, give him this specific time, specific place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We take issue with that. Again "specific" is of course a relative term based on the type of crime which a particular case involves. So if the accused's actions which result in criminal liability occurred over a five or six month period and that is the relative period, the Prosecution cannot say, well, we are only going to pick one day, nor should it be required to say we are only going to pick one day, of discrete activity, when the substance of crime was committed over this entire period.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you leave the vagueness part of your position, I do want to ask you a question, so I will let you finish the vagueness, then you tell me and I will ask you a question about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I have expressed the essential points.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The only reference that Mr. Wladimiroff makes to the amended indictment in saying that it fails to meet its responsibility is count 1. There are 36 counts and his only reference, and specific reference and challenge, is count 1. As I was looking at counts 1, 2 and 3 and then I went on to read counts 4 through 36, it seemed to me that each of the counts other than 1 through 3 had specific dates. For example, if you look at count 4 there is an exact date: "In early June 1992". Then it says: "Sometime between early June and August 3rd 1992". Then if you look at 6 it says: "Between June 1st and July 31st." So in each of the counts, other than 1 through 3, there are specific dates mentioned. The only challenge that Mr. Wladimiroff has specifically mentioned today is count 1. Paragraph 4 which accompanies counts 1, 2 and 3 says: "Between May 23rd 1992 and December 31st 1992". As I read the indictment it was my interpretation that the specifics, in terms of specific dates, were set out in counts 4 through 36. Then after you look at all of those specific dates you then sort of return to counts 1 through 3, and at least in the proof -- I have no idea how you will offer this proof -- of counts 1, 2 and 3 you will be relying on the proof that you have offered in counts 4 through 36. Am I totally incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I took Mr. Wladimiroff's discussion of the first counts as merely an example. I presumed from his motion that he would take issue with most of the counts in the same way in some version or another.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I am saying is that it is only counts 1 through 3 that have this global reference of May 23rd 1992 through December 31st 1992, and all of the other counsel there are monthly dates specifically mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: There are some others that are a bit more broad. For example, paragraph 6 is June to 31st July. The issue here, as I said, the description of the relevant facts, and he used the term "specific facts", is a relevant term depending on the type of charge. In that first count we would not be relying solely on the dates and offences in the other counts in the indictment for that counts 1 through 3. So it is not limited specifically to the other counts in the indictment. The point is, for the charge of the crime against humanity based on persecution, the relevant acts committed were committed throughout that period, so that is, if you will, a specific date for that particular crime. As I said, "specific" is a relative term. If the Prosecution's submission is that that is the relative time for the commission of this offence, and brings forth that proof, the Defence cannot be heard to demand from the Prosecution that it selects one day in a series of acts which are all relative to a particular crime and limit us to the proof of one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you something about persecution? There is an odd feature, is there not, about the very act of persecution that necessarily it would not seem likely to be one event, but it is a general course of conduct that amounts to a persecution and inherently, therefore, it extends over a period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it potentially could be one specific event in the right case, or again it could occur as alleged here over a lengthy period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Normally you think of persecution as being a continuing situation, but that is not so, for instance, with count 3, unlawful deportation or transfer or confinement, that can be one simple act. So that it was perhaps unfortunate that persecution was chosen by Mr. Wladimiroff as the instance, because it lends itself to a lengthy period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: But the converse of course is if a number of deportations occurred over a period of time and in a sense it is one course of conduct, then it is relevant to one charge but over a lengthy period of time.
