The point of this is that any these offences can occur both discretely or within a related series of events, and if the proof indicates it is such then it is a relevant charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I doubt that myself. I can understand one act of deportation, but I cannot imagine one act being described as the crime of persecution on political grounds. Be that as it may, it is a peculiar feature of the offence of persecution I suppose. You say really the ability to put up an effective defence is quite irrelevant to this motion, because that is something that comes after the indictment and in the course of discovery?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct. In the Tribunal's system, in its process, yes. The indictment serves the purpose of notifying the accused of the charges such that the accused can then enter pleas. Then our process allows for the continuation of the provision of information to the Defence, such that it can meet the requirement to provide adequate facilities for the preparation of a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is more we are quite unable to determine anything about that because we know nothing about the material that has been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That particular issue, yes, sir. The Defence in fact in his argument stated that the crime of persecution as to count 1 has not been described as an individual event, but as a combination of other events. Then he listed out of course the acts. They said that is what they understood this to say; all we know is that a persecution took place in the Opstina of Prijedor during this period and it consisted of these acts. That is exactly the point. That is the crime, elements of the crime which we are alleging. So in fact the indictment did serve its purpose. It provided them the notice of exactly what it was intended to. The issue of concurrence of charges, as I stated earlier, we believe this indictment does not contain an unreasonable concurrence or multiplication of charges and nor does it expose the accused to double jeopardy. The principle set forth in Rule 49 of the Tribunal Rules contains also within it an inherent corollary to the Rule that a series of related acts committed by an accused can be joined in a single indictment. That is, that a single act committed by an accused which violates multiple criminal provisions may also be brought in a single indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I read that in your submission. Of course, you were not with us when we were drafting these rules, but I suppose an argument could be made that if that was the intent we would have a rule following 49, because 49 says that two or more crimes may be joined in one indictment. If the series of acts committed together form the same transaction, then the said crimes were committed by the same accused, is count 1 a different crime than count 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The corollary, you say the inherent corollary is what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Because, as 49 could be read to read that a series of acts, if the series of acts committed together form the same transaction, then the said crimes were committed by accused. The corollary to that is if it is the same act in a discrete instance violated more than one criminal provision, those multiple crimes could also be alleged in the same indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Assuming that is true then, should they be alleged as concurrent crimes or alternatively?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We believe they should be alleged as discrete and concurrent crimes. We believe that provision is recognised in a number of jurisdictions, including the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the Former Yugoslavia, as well as a number of other countries which we cited in our brief. The determining factor appears to be the intent in those individual countries of the legislature when you look at the citations and the discussions to those provisions in the relevant criminal codes. If it was intended that the crimes be separate crimes, be considered separately, then separate convictions can stand even though they are based on the same conduct. In the present indictment each general paragraph is structured to address a particular instance or course of conduct. Then set forth in the counts are the crimes violating the provision of Articles 2, 3 and 5 in this particular indictment, which the conduct of the accused meets. In articles 2, 3 and 5 there are particular crimes listed with similar descriptive titles. For example, Article 2(a) wilful killing; Article 3 murder, Article 5(a) murder. These crimes have at their root a common act or a course of conduct. That is not to say, however, that they are the same offence. Articles 2, 3 and 5 are distinct and separate categories of offences with separate requirements, elements and purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, what is the difference between an offence and a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: A crime ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I am using the term interchangeably in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So they are different crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. They have at their root, if you will, a particular crime, murder, but that is not to say that because one basic act may be similar, that the offence, the crime under our Statute between Articles 2, 3 and 5 are the same.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They may not be the same crime because different elements may need to be established. For example, in a crime against humanity you would have that widespread systematic, but you would not have another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Again I just wonder whether they are the same crime, the same offence or whether they truly are different crimes because of the requirement of a different element, but I do not know what difference that makes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: My point was I was centering on the basic act. In all three of the Articles you have an act that accounts for individual murders, but beyond that issue of the actual commission of the murder there are other required elements and that is because they are in fact separate crimes, even though the basic act may be the murder of the same person or persons. We believe that because there are distinct requirements, elements and purposes, that it is possible for one act of murder to violate all three articles. If so then the accused, if guilty, should stand responsible for violating all three, and the separate principle for which they stand. The consideration of multiple convictions is generally given at the time of sentencing as mentioned by the Defence in its argument, which is an issue which is not appropriate for the question whether the offences can be alleged in the indictment and stand for trial. Article 2 in our present Statute is intended to address violations of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Convention of 1949. The object and purpose of the grave breach provisions is to govern specific aspects of the conduct of armed conflicts and protect certain groups of persons in particular. As stated in the commentary to the Fourth Geneva Convention, the main object of the Fourth Geneva Convention is to protect a strictly defined category of civilians from arbitrary action on the part of the enemy and not from the dangers of military operations in general. The fundamental principles of the laws and customs of war enumerated in the language of common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and embraced by Article 3 of our Statute, provide the minimum rules of conduct applicable to all armed conflicts regardless of classification. These minimum rules cover a wider class of actor and protect a wider category of persons than the grave breach provisions. They are essential rules of humanity recognised by all civilised nations and their purpose is to ensure the humane and non-discriminatory treatment of all non-combatants or persons not involved in the armed conflict. To do so, they established the benchmark rules applicable to all armed conflicts that must be observed in each instance without derogation. Then Article 5 of the Statute addresses crimes against humanity. The principal purposes of crimes against humanity has no relation in its core to the conduct of armed conflicts. Rather, it is to ensure the right of diverse parts of civilian populations to exist. An essential element of the crimes against humanity is the protection of the members of a civilian population from a widespread and systematic attack. Because each of these articles has a distinct purpose and object and, as a consequence, contain different elements, it is permissible that they be charged together in an instance where a particular act is violative of each. And the accused, if guilty, should be subject to the conviction for each. It may well be again for purposes of sentencing that the various offences are merged for unified sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. I missed what you were reading from then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir, as to which part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What you have just quoted; that is a quotation from something, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, sir, that is just my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I had missed a valuable authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The essential point inherent in allowing for multiple convictions is that each crime exists to protect certain society norms, and each must be valued and preserved. Each of the Articles charged in the indictment represent the most serious of offences. There is a significant interest for the community of nations to ensure that the purpose and prohibitions of each Article is respected and are prosecuted in the instance where the evidence warrants. There should be no instance where an accused should free from the responsibility for violating one of these offences simply because his or her conduct is also violative of one of the other articles as well. There should be no issues of expediency or economy where one of these offences is concerned. If there is a consolidation for sentencing purposes, then there is no significant prejudice to the accused, yet the interests of the community of nations in preserving the purposes of these Articles is respected. That is all I have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is fine. Are there further questions? Mr. Wladimiroff, I have a few questions, if I may? As I listened to your presentation, you did focus on count 1, 2 and 3 and you pointed out what you considered to be the failures in terms of vagueness of those counts. Did you mean also to specifically refer the Chamber to the other counts and, if so, how could you point out what vagueness there is in the other counts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I may try to do so. I just used paragraph 4 as an example and confined myself to count 1. Let me just briefly indicate what the problems may be if I refer to the other paragraphs. Paragraph 5, the time frame related to the alleged rape is not early June 1992, but early June and 3rd August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Between June and August 3rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. So that is a very large time frame to decide the issue when did that happen and in what time frame should we interview witnesses, and if a witness says that in a specific week or days something might have happened to establish an alibi, to find other witnesses to tell us that Mr. Tadic was not there, for example. You see, that is one of the main problems here. The behaviour of Tadic has not been described. The place, I think, is not a real problem. It is inside the Separacija so that is pretty clear. If I now look into paragraph 6 -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, let me make sure I understand then your position: Paragraph 5 which accompanies counts 4, 5 and 6 states: "Between early June and August 3rd 1992". Let me step back a moment. Let me ask you then what is the standard that should be applied in determining whether or not the indictment is not vague? Is it to inform the accused of the nature of the offences charged, or did I understand you correctly that it should be something more, that it should be a unique and factual description of the crime and his participation? If so, what is your legal basis for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The legal basis for that, your Honour, is that in Article 21, paragraph 4, we learn that we are dealing with minimum guarantees. If the Statute says that the accused should be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and the cause of charges charged against him, I may stress again, minimum guarantees. So what does it mean? It has, apparently, been adopted from the International Covenant -- it has already been debated also by the Prosecution, that if we focus on to Article 14(3)(a), there we see the same wording, though it says that the meaning of it is not only the exact legal description of the offence, but also the facts underlying it. So, it is not only the nature of the legal allegation: "Sir, you have committed a murder, period", but it should also point out the facts underlaying that legal allegation, explaining to the accused where, when and under which circumstances that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is where I, perhaps, have some difficulty, where, when and under what circumstances it happened. Where is that standard set out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The underlaying facts of an offence, because there are those facts that may establish the criminal provision, that may constitute a crime. Just saying: "Sir, you raped someone" or just "you killed someone" is a legal issue, because what is killing? That debate will be somewhat later because then we have to debate what is the difference between -- I hesitate to say it -- an ordinary killing and a war crime? That difference has also a factual meaning. So we should learn about the facts underlaying the offence, you see. The facts are decisive, where do we deal with an ordinary killing or a war crime? The facts are also decisive to determine: Has he, the Prosecution, accused me of that event or another offence? Which offence should I defend myself to? Is it something that happened in June or was it something that happened in July? If they say it was in June, how can I establish I was not there to find witnesses? We should have something which is more precise; not a very large range of places and times and a non-description of the actual behaviour. We do not know whether we should look at Mr. Tadic on the basis of the indictment as a principal or someone who aided and abetted to the crime. We do not know. It was just participation in; what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So as to paragraph 5 where it says "sometime between early June and 3rd August 1992", you would want a particular date, June 5th, July 10th or something like that? That is what is required, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that it may not be possible to fix one date, but I think the Prosecution should have done better by interviewing F by limiting the time frame to make the accused clear what we are talking about. They may have done, and then this information is not disclosed in the indictment, that is the basis of the trial, or they may not have done and for that reason we do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you rely on Article 21 of the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Article 21(4) is concerned with the determination of any charge against the accused, which is quite distinct from Article 18(4) which is concerned with the preparation of indictment. As one would expect, they contain different standards. 18(4) requires a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the man is charged or the woman is charged; whereas Article 21, dealing with the much later, in this case very much later, case of the determination of a charge, there you have to have in detail the nature and cause of the charge. I am, at all events, quite unable to look forward to the situation that is dealt with in Article 21, namely, the determination of a charge, because I know nothing about what additional material has been supplied as required by the Rules which have been, as I understand it, complied with, the evidence that is going to be given by the various witnesses. For all I know, F in paragraph 5 of the indictment may in the material that has been given to you specify in the most precise way what the date was. Your complaint really is not concerned with the indictment so much as your ability to put up a defence. That is something that is not appropriate for this motion. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We take a different view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is a delightfully tactful way of putting it!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As we see it, your Honour, Article 18, paragraph 4, is not a different standard from Article 21, paragraph 4 again, because these two provisions are not independent to each other. They depend on each other because you will not be able to determine any charge if there is not an appropriate charge in the indictment. The difference of view between the Prosecution and the Defence is that we do not see the indictment simply as a notice, and from there to supply the Defence with more information that makes it possible in the ongoing process of the trial to understand what is meant in the indictment so that, at the end of the day, the Defence will be in a position to understand what was meant in the indictment, so, at the end of the day, we may or may not be able to determine the charge in the indictment; we take the position that from the very day of the indictment, we should be in the position to understand what is the exact nature of the charge, not in legal terms only, but also in factual terms. That is, as we see it, the minimum guarantee in the International Covenant because the Covenant does not only deal with Anglo-Saxon criminal systems but also with Continental systems. So, we have here a blended system which is melted into the Statute. We believe that in the system of the Statute the indictment should not be seen as a simple notice, because in the system of the Statute such a simple notice would not be sufficient to allow the Defence to fulfil its obligations to file specific motions, if there is any reason to do so, within a period of 60 days.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But I think Judge Stephen's point is, as it relates to this, that in determination of a charge, that is not something that the Defence counsel does, that is something that the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that Article 21(4) when it says "in determination of any charge", it then states a number of things, including the right to be tried without undue delay, the right to be tried in the presence, etc. So the determination comes later and with the benefit of more evidence, so to speak. Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I made out that that is the position of Defence. Of course, it is your task to determine what is the charge, but is it not essential for an accused to understand what he is charged of in order to enable him to determine what is the nature of that charge in legal terms and in factual terms, because without that understanding, not being in a position to determine what is the charge, what is then the use of paragraphs A, B, C, D, E, F and G of paragraph 4? That will be without any sense, if it was not for the accused to understand, but for the Trial Chamber to understand. Both will have to be able to determine what is going on. So, it is our obligation from the very beginning to understand what is the nature of the charge in legal terms and in factual terms to determine what is the charge we should defend. For that reason, I pointed out that from the very beginning you have to be able to deal, for example, with the obligations under the Rules to fulfil the possibility of motions within 60 days. If you are not able to do so, then the indictment is not a proper basis of a trial. We cannot simply during the ongoing process of the trial by discovery through cross-examination discover also, "Now I understand it was not an allegation manned through that event, but now we see that the Prosecutor is heading for another event". It should be clear from the very moment that we are dealing with the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not want to argue this matter with you, but can I just see what your reaction is to this fact, that it is quite clear, is it not, from looking at the Statute that the two Articles, 18 and 21, lay down different standards? 18, which deals with the situation when a prime facie case has been determined to exist, merely calls for a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged. Very different is the requirement in the determination of any charge, that is, at the trial, there must have been a situation in which under (a) of 21(4) in detail an understanding of the nature and cause of the charge against him. Those are two different standards. They are stated to apply at different times and you are necessarily concerned only with the first of those two standards in 18(4). Have you any anything to say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to do so, your Honour, because we feel that there is no inconsistency or no difference in standard in 18 and 21. Different to your approach, we do not separate in time an understanding of those provisions. I beg your pardon if I say that it is an absolute Anglo-Saxon approach. I doubt whether this is under the Statute the approach that was meant to be the proceedings in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does not the European Court of Human Rights take the same view?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, because they are dealing with different systems. For example -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But they are dealing with a different document which lays down the same criteria, though, and quite distinctly deals with two different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It may be even more complicated. The European Court looked afterwards, what has become from these minimum guarantees in the context of a national system? In some systems, it is accepted that the criteria laid down in the International Covenants are taken in two steps, for example, in the Anglo-Saxon system, but in the continental system it does not. So, the issue here is, is the Statute providing us with a pure Anglo-Saxon system to be judged as a two-step issue and then, if that is true, 18 provides a further step and 21 in the second step. We take the position that if you look into the Rules and you look into what the Prosecution and the Defence will have to do in the system of rules, we understand the Rules as being one step. From the very beginning the indictment should be clear because it is the unique basis of everything that goes on after that date it has been issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is very helpful and I fully understand your position now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We hope, Mr. Wladimiroff, or I do believe that the Judges tried to take the best of both systems, both Anglo-Saxon system and the civil law systems, and there are differences. We have 10 rules of evidence, for example. In the Anglo-Saxon system, certainly in the American system, there are rules and rules and rules, and we have not done that. Then the role of the Appeals Chamber is very different in our Rules than in the Anglo-Saxon system. We have tried to take the best of both possible worlds. I am sure that we will have other criticisms saying: "Well, this is a civil law system rule, and this is not the way that it is done in the Anglo-Saxon system". That may be true because we have combined both, but in the process there has to be a give and take.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not criticised the Anglo-Saxon system; I am just saying that in my assessment of the Rules and the Statute we have a blended version here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, without going through each and every count, I gather that all of them -- I do not think that any count gives a specific date -- give a range of June 1st through to July 31st; another one says around July 10th 1992, that is paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: For example, that will not be a problem but there are three issues: When, where or what? The "whens" are sometimes very vague and refer to a spacious time frame and some are not. "Where" is in many cases very vague in, some cases not. In any of the charges the "what", the question of what was the behaviour of Dusko Tadic, what was his part, his culpable part, in the events is absolutely vague and certainly not specified per count.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, our Rules, Rule 66, provides that "the Prosecutor shall on request permit the defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects in his custody or control, which are material to the preparation of the defence, or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial or were obtained from or belonged to the accused". That is tremendously broad. So, it seems to me that what the Prosecutor has, if you request it, they will give you all of the documents that are material to the preparation of the defence, or which were intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial. We talked about that, I guess, and then that triggers this reciprocal discovery, I suppose. That is, if you make that request, then under our Rules, then the Prosecutor would be entitled to inspect any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects which are within the custody or control of the Defence, and which he intends to use as evidence at the trial. So, you may not want to make that request because then there is a reciprocal obligation on your part. But if it is made, and if that reciprocity comes into being, then each side will have much, much more, I think, than they would have in many, many Anglo-Saxon systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think that is not the issue, your Honour, if you please, because that would be a step 1.5 between step 1 and step 2. What we argue is that from the very moment the indictment has been issued and read to the accused, from that moment on, we should understand what is the nature, the factual nature, of the allegation; we should not discover that later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that and I have heard the colloquy between you and Judge Stephen. But what the Prosecutor says is then if you look to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and look to Article 14, then it speaks of this initial document, but it also speaks of supplementary materials that may enable more. What I am suggesting is by pointing to these Rules, this is an example of supplementary materials that will enable almost an open book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that, but it may not solve the problems we have been discussing. Maybe Mr. Orie will add something to this point?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: On this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: On this point, on this specific issue. If it pleases, your Honour, it is a matter of principle. It is not a matter of how to solve our problem in how to prepare the Defence. That is one of the consequences of the problem. I will just try to give you an example. Let us just assume that the charge is murder: "You murdered within one month Mr. X". I do not know whether I am supposed to have strangled Mr. X; whether I am supposed to have beaten him down with an axe or that I have poisoned him. Of course, if I have access to the material, the idea is that it would become clearer to me what actually happened. But let us just assume that the material (and there is a lot of material that has been exchanged that you might know) is contradictory. If it is contradicting itself, if, for example -- of course, this is not reality -- one of the witnesses says: "Well, he strangled Mr. X" and the other says: "He poisoned him", then I still have no guideline for my defence, because what should I do? Should I investigate the availability of axes in the area during that period of time which might be a very suitable defence if I was supposed to have slain Mr. X with an axe; or should I investigate the availability of poison, or should I investigate whether my hands were paralysed at that moment because of an illness so I could not have strangled him? It is not just a matter of how to solve the Defence problems; it is a matter of principle as well. The Defence says that we are entitled to know in more detail, good enough to prepare a defence -- of course, that is one of the consequences -- the character, both factual and legal, of the crime. Just by paying attention to the practical solution of the problems, this is not good enough. I gave you one of the very strong reasons for it, that if the supporting material is contradictory in itself, and it might be here and there, then we still do not know how to prepare the defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There, I gather, then in the Dutch system where you practise that would be provided, that is, in the indictment it would say the date that it occurred and specifically how it occurred, so when, where and what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, if there is a rape charge, under Dutch law they have to describe what kind of force has been used, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There would be the exact date, the exact way it was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As good as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There we are, with the "good as possible".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I do understand that if you say it is around 10th July, then, of course, this gives us a far better idea. I think you always can ask from the Prosecution to describe as precise as possible under that circumstances. But if you say it was just rape in a period of two months -- for example, it might be known -- I am not referring to the case -- that it was during a weekend which is, of course, of major importance for the Defence because they have to find people who were, perhaps, working in camps during weekends. So if this is known it should be in there and -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I am trying to find out. That is what is provided in the Dutch system? The Dutch system would require then that there be a specific date and a description of how it was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think it is of little use to refer to the Dutch system.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am following your lead actually when you suggested Anglo-Saxon. Now I am looking at civil -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dutch is not everything; it is not Anglo-Saxon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I know it is not; that is why I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In any civil law systems you will find in most systems a requirement of providing such factual information. Of course, there are differences, for example, between Netherlands and Germany and France, but the heart of the matter is you have to provide the factual information that enables the accused to defend himself, not at a later stage but to start with in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that. I am trying to focus on what is the level of factuality, if that is a word, that is required in civil law systems that is lacking in our discussion about our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think Mr. Vujin will enlighten on that, how it works in the former Yugoslavia which might be an appropriate guideline how to deal in this case. MR. VUJIN (original: Serbian): Your Honour, I must say straightaway that if we would look at this from the point of view of Yugoslav criminal legislation, then this indictment could not be seriously criticised in terms of the institutes existing in Yugoslav criminal law, namely, according to Article 262 of the law on criminal procedure, the indictment must contain a description of the crime which gives the elements, the legal elements, of the crime, the time and place when the crime was committed, the object that was used and the tool that was used, and other circumstances needed for determining the act as specifically as possible. That is what the Defence pointed to on this occasion as well. If we look at the indictment as it is, it is not in keeping with B Rule 47 of the Rules of Procedure where it says that it has to contain information under facts related thereto, as brief information does not mean that information should not be provided. You give facts briefly, as is the case in the criminal legislation of the former and present Yugoslavia and of the Republic of Srpske. What I wish to say, by the way, is that people talk about the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina here too. On behalf of the defendant, I kindly request you not to refer to that law here because he does not belong to that State; he belongs, in fact, although this State is not recognised internationally, to the state of the Republic of Srpske which has all the attributes of a state, which has a law of its own and applies this law. So, the defendant, Dusko Tadic, cannot fall under the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but only under the jurisdiction of the Republic of Srpske.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, I do not know when that was said, but I attempt to say, at least, former Yugoslavia. Maybe it was the Prosecutor. When we are speaking we say "former Yugoslavia" which is a better, more inclusive term. MR. VUJIN (original: Serbian): This remark does not pertain to the attitude of the Trial Chamber and of your Honour personally, but it pertains to the Prosecution. According to our point of view, as we take paragraph B of Rule 47, the indictment must contain the description of how the crime was committed, that is to say, the exact time with more or less latitude and the way in which it was committed and also the tool that was used as described by Mr. Orie. Why is this important? If we look only briefly at count 6 of the changed indictment, of the amended indictment, when you speak of the period "from June 1st to July 31st a group of Serbs, including Dusko Tadic, had beaten up several times a group of prisoners, including Emir Karabasic and others ... and after that Karabasic, Hrnic, Alic and Harambasic died as a result of the assaults. By his participation in these acts Dusko Tadic committed". It says "by his participation"; there is no description as to how he participated, if he did, how they were beaten up, with what tool, with what implement, did he actually have access to this, was he only present, was he in command, did he beat somebody up, who did he beat up, somebody from the group or these four people who died later as a result? Because, according to the material we have received from the Prosecution now, we do not have any information or any proof that these people had died eventually. I am not trying to prejudge anything. I am just trying to explain why we need this additional information. Therefore, the indictment has to contain such things in keeping with 47(B). I just wish to add in terms of the several counts concerning the same crime, they speak of Article 248 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, that a perpetrator of several crimes does not give the right to the Prosecution to qualify the acts of Dusko Tadic by several crimes. Also, if you look at Rule 49 of the Rules of Procedure, they are not entitled to do that, if you look at the joinder of crimes. I wish to add something else: On previous occasions we have pointed out that the Statute of this Tribunal was adopted in contrast to the basic principles of international criminal law, and that is that it prescribes responsibility, criminal liability, for acts committed before this enactment was passed. The basic maxim being that nobody can be accused for a crime which was not stipulated by law before that. The question is, if this is applied, and if you, as a court, should try on that basis and if you find that you can try on the basis of a Statute that was passed in 1993, and it looks back at the period starting with 1991, are you supposed to try people, according to the Geneva Convention, the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, and to do at the same time something that is stipulated by the Geneva Conventions and by the Statute of the Trial Chamber? If you find that you can try only according to the Statute of the Tribunal, then it is only the crimes that are stipulated in the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, if you do not wish to discuss further the portion of your motion dealing with vagueness, I had a question with respect to that section of the motion that deals with the concurrence of charges. My question is, how are you prejudiced by the joinder of these multiple crimes in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me try to say this as follows, your Honour: In essence, there are two ways to deal with this problem, or there are provisions in your law that provide for a regulation of problems of concurrence if so in the indictment, and when deciding on what has been proven and, therefore, when the Judges go to qualify what is a charge, or a system provides rules that deal with the same problem but then on the level of sentencing. As far as I understand, in most systems it is one of either ways. So, a normal coherent system, there is answer to this question, and then the Defence would not have raised it. But here, in the system of the Statute and the Rules, there is no answer to the issue of concurrence if we talk about the indictment. There is no answer to the issue of concurrence if we talk about what will be the qualification of the Judges if one act may result in multiple crimes, and the rules only say if we look into sentencing that you should deal with the guidelines for sentencing of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Am I correct then that the code in the former Yugoslavia allows for the inclusion of concurrent additional crimes? It allows a Prosecutor to plead concurrently as opposed to alternatively?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then our Article, then our Statute and our Rules say that we are to take into consideration for sentencing purposes the sentencing procedures of the former Yugoslavia, so could we not then do that? What we would be taking into consideration is a system of pleading that is allowed as well as a system of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the Defence may rely on such a position, then I think that will clarify a lot of the problems. If we are sure that at the end of the day you will apply the Yugoslav rules in such a way that it will not be possible to punish Dusko Tadic for each crime, though being the result of one act, then we are quite satisfied. But the rules do not supply us with that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If, though, the Prosecutor were required to plead alternatively, as you suggest should be the system, do you not then possibly run into the same problem at the time of sentencing, that is, that they say that it violated the Geneva Convention or, in the alternative, laws and customs of war or, in the alternative, crimes against humanity, and we may find that they violated all, so can that not be accomplished whether it is pled alternatively or pled separately, if I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Each alternative excludes the other one, that is, A or B. If you say it is A, that will be decisive for your sentencing. One might say, alternatively, maybe a better phrase would be using as a subsidiary, but that is more, I am afraid, a civil law word that might be quite difficult to translate into the Anglo-Saxon system. It simply means that if you chose for one qualification, the other ones are excluded for sentencing purposes. If we are confident that a Trial Chamber will follow that system, at the end of the day, we regret that we cannot anticipate on that system by reading the indictment, but, well, a lot of our fears and problems will be solved, of course. We rather prefer to have an indictment that makes clear that it is or A, or B, or C, but not altogether, because then you start with the most severe one in normal systems, then if it is not murder, you go down to killing, if it is not killing, you go down to manslaughter and so on. But that is very difficult in this case because there no rules related to each crime in terms of that crime has that maximum of so many years. There is nothing in the Rules; it seems all equal. So we do not know what you will choose.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do our Rules, in your opinion, provide for -- particularly Rule 49 -- the indicting of more than one crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 49 does not say that a joinder of crime is possible as a result of one act. It leaves the question open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, can I ask you one question? You mentioned Article 49 of the Yugoslav code. We do not have a copy of Article 49. What you said about it sounded interesting. Could we have an English translation of it, or could you, perhaps, provide us with the original in the original language and we can have it translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) I am afraid that we have not understood each other correctly. I did not speak of Article 49 of the Yugoslav law. I spoke of Rule 49 of the Rules of this Tribunal. I spoke of Article 48. I think you have a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have 48. I thought you were referring to the next Article, 49, which we have not got, but you were not. Thank you. In that case, my question is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) Yes, but I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to respond in a way to the question raised by the presiding Judge, why we are opposed to several counts. In Yugoslav criminal law, when we are talking of cases such as the one mentioned in count 6, that is, beatings, murder etc., there is a provision whereby the graver offence consummates the lower one. So, the court cannot declare a person guilty of murder or abuse of any kind, because all of that is consummated by the act of murder. So, if somebody is convicted of murder, then it is the only conviction that you can have, not for all the other offences.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I recall, I do believe that we considered when we were drafting the Rules, the lesser included offences, it was suggested by some countries, parties, but that is not what we have chosen. Let me suggest this, though, if it is your fear -- my question, really, was how are you prejudiced -- that the way that the indictment is drafted will result in an illegal sentencing basically, I think that can be corrected -- I think this was Judge Stephen's point some time ago -- by an appropriate sentence. No matter how the Prosecutor chooses to frame its indictment, that does not justify the Chamber, should find that Mr. Tadic is guilty of any of the counts. of sentencing illegally. There are separate rules that govern our sentencing as well as, as I said, the recent appeals decision on jurisdiction ---

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) I hope so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- gives us some guidance too. So, if that is your fear, I do not want to suggest that you trust us -- that would not be fair to you -- but what I would suggest is that the two do not necessarily go hand-in-hand. Our sentencing process is dictated by our Rules. You have made reference to 101. That is where we will be guided. It just seems to be premature at this time. That is why I was trying to focus on what was your prejudice. How do you feel that you are prejudiced by this form of indictment, not the vagueness, but the way that it is crafted and that is containing different crimes growing out of the same series of acts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have made reference, your Honour, to Rule 101. But, as you may recall, we are not sure whether the reference to the general practice regarding prison sentencing in the course of the former Yugoslavia fully addresses the problem we have raised. That depends on the second step which is not in the Rules which you mentioned here in the courtroom, that is, that if you choose for a concurrence realis and not for a concurrence idealis, because in a concurrence idealis one offence absolves all the others, but if you choose for a concurrence realis, all crimes can be separately on the table, although being the result of one act, then the sentencing guidelines of the former Yugoslavia does not address that problem. But if you tell us that you read the Rules in such a way that you will only sentence as it was just one being a concurrence idealis, then we have no problem. But to start with, it is not in the rules, we do not know what your policy will be in this matter, so we argue to start with that it should be in the indictment because then we have a guarantee. If it is not in the indictment, it is a credit to the court. We have no problem in giving you all the credit we have -- and that is a lot, your Honour -- but we want to be sure that this is not a problem that will turn out to be a real problem at the end of trial when he has already been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it were pled alternatively, you are saying we would have no choice but to sentence on one or the other but not both?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me, your Honour, just to make a short remark as far as Rule 49 is concerned? You asked Mr. Wladimiroff whether this would give an answer to the problem. He said it left it open whether Rule 49 dealt with the situation of multiple acts or one act falling within the scope of several provisions of a criminal code. I think, as a matter of fact, that it would not have been necessary to incorporate the last line of 49 if this Rule was dealing with one act falling within the scope of several criminal provisions, because it is committed by the same accused. If we were talking about one act, it would not be necessary to stress that it was committed by the same accused because, from a logical point of view, in my view, the reading of Rule 49 makes clear that this is dealing with the situation of several different acts and not with one act falling within the scope of several provisions of criminal law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the purpose of that phrase in Rule 49 was to distinguish it from Rule 48 that talks about the joinder of persons. So, what we were trying to say in Rule 49, if we are here talking about joinder of crimes, in the previous Rule we are talking about joinder of more than one accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) However, with your permission, your Honour, look at Article 49, this is in the indictment and we are not opposed to that, because there are several acts that constitute several crimes, but now we are talking about one act. The Prosecutor should decide what is the one crime that he accuses Dusko Tadic of. That is 47(B). It is quite clear in 47(B) that it has to be one crime, the crime. You speak in the singular. It is "crime", not "crimes". Therefore, he has to be accused of having committed one crime.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have anything further with respect to your motion on the form of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I do not think so except for some reiteration of what I have just previously said, that is, that we would unlikely end up with a case if your Chamber might find Mr. Tadic guilty, which we do not believe, but if so, we would not like him to be sentenced for 500 years, 600 years, as seems to be the case in countries where there is this concurrence realis.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, do you have anything further to add to your response? Please feel free as you wish to speak for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes ma'am. First, I would like, of course, to cite paragraph 36 of the Report of the Secretary General, just on the issue of what influence any particular national system should have. That paragraph clearly indicates that there is only one related issue which would require reference to domestic practice and that is, namely, penalties which, of course, indicates that the Trial Chamber would have reference to the law of the former Yugoslavia. It does not indicate, of course, that it is actually bound by it, but simply that it should refer to it. So, we believe that the issue of what one particular system may require in our indictments as opposed to another is not particularly relevant to this determination. The relevant determination here is what do our Statute and Rules require. Judge Stephen, I believe the other provision of Yugoslavia in the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina which, of course, is the site of the crimes, which is why it may be relevant, is Article 262 which you do have in your package which states the requirements for the indictment with the other facet which Mr. Vujin cited. But, in any event, the question really before this Tribunal, this whole issue of concurrence of offences, is the balance of the right of the accused to have a fair trial, of course, against the right of the community of nations to ensure that the principles of international humanitarian law are respected. As I cited earlier, we believe that that interest would mandate that the charges not be pled or found in the alternative, but if the actions of the accused warrants a conviction on any particular Article, then it should be so, and not this alternative pleading, and that any prejudice to the accused would be dealt with in the sentencing process. Of course, that is a matter which, as you said earlier, can be taken up at a later time and is not relevant to this particular hearing. That is all I have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I do not want to repeat so I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for lunch until 2.30 and we will return at that time. (Luncheon adjournment) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We would like to proceed with the Defence's motion on non-bis-in-idem, if we can, please? Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am, your Honour. I feel a bit more at ease than perhaps my colleague Mr. Wladimiroff this morning, your Honours, because I at least deal with an issue that is dealt with by the Statute and the Rules of Procedure as well, unlike the concursus idealis of this morning. The Appeals Chamber has dealt with the issue of primacy of jurisdiction. That was in the circumstances where the Defence had argued that creating an ad hoc Tribunal vested with jurisdiction of a primary nature was beyond the powers of the Security Council. The argument then had a rather elevated level of abstraction. While dealing with the motion of non bis in idem, and of course there is a certain link between the primacy of jurisdiction and the non bis in idem issue, I cannot avoid a certain level of abstraction as well, but I will come down to the specific aspects of this case especially as far as the deferral of this case is concerned. It seems to me that the motion of Defence on the non bis in idem might not have been fully understood by the Prosecution. Therefore, I would like to clarify, first, what the motion does not intend to say. At the same time this exercise will make clear in how far the Defence agrees with the Prosecution's response on some issues of a rather legal, technical nature. After having eliminated these misunderstandings, perhaps they are also due to our struggle to invent not just one wheel but quite a lot of wheels in this procedure, I will explain to you is what is the core argument of the motion and why we felt we had to file it. I will start with the classical concept of non bis in idem or as, in American language, it is usually said double jeopardy or, in English, autre fois convict, autre fois acquit, I must say it is excellent wording from the English because it solves the problem of the rivalry between languages in this Tribunal a bit, the English wordings being French. The classical concept of non bis in idem -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But not pronounced at all as the French pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I know that. I do not know exactly how you pronounce it, but I still feel the French in it. The classical concept of non bis in idem seeks to protect a person from being tried for a second time for the same criminal acts. Apart from the substantive aspect that a person should not be punished twice and serve a second sentence for the same offence, it also has a procedural aspect. Double jeopardy does not only bar a double punishment but also a double prosecution. The concept of non bis in idem originally was limited in its scope and only covered a double prosecution within one State, within one jurisdiction. The Rule protected only a person identical to the one previously put in jeopardy for acts identical to the ones he was charged with before and against a prosecuting authority identical to the one that had prosecuted him before. The requirement of both parties had to be identical to the parties in the previous prosecution gave the principle of non bis in idem its original narrow, domestic scope. A previous prosecution, for example, in Spain did not deprive, for example, the German authorities from exercising the jurisdiction they had been vested with under German domestic law. We even see nowadays that the principle is functioning similarly in many constitutions and domestic laws. If I may refer to the 5th amendment in the United States, or Article 103(3) of the German constitution, we see that they have been consistently interpreted as only protecting against a second prosecution within the same jurisdiction. The Defence agrees with the Prosecution that Article 14, section 7, of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the same is true for Article 4 of the 7th Protocol to the European Convention on Human Rights, that these rules cannot be interpreted as being applicable beyond the domestic context, although one might find some uncertainty in the past as to the scope of operation of Article 14, section 7, of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. There is no sound authority to rely upon for assuming an international operation of these provisions. Of course, there is an international operation but not international from the point of view of non bis in idem. The underlying idea of the non bis in idem principle is not much helped, however, and neither is the individual involved by the classical theory of sovereignty of States resulting in no obligation whatsoever to respect foreign judgment as a bar to a second prosecution. One can observe that many States have sought to protect the individual to the extent that this protection was compatible with the interest of that particular sovereign State. What we then find as a result in domestic legal provisions is that they often grant a limited protection against a double prosecution by different States. I may just refer as an example, not because it is everything beyond Anglo-Saxon law, but Article 68 of the Dutch criminal code and, for example, case law in the United Kingdom, Archbold Criminal Pleading in Evidence Practice in its 1993 edition refers, for example, to a recent case of R. v. Lavercombe and Murray (1988). The kind of limitation -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is Lavercombe and Murray. The kind of, I would say, self-imposed limitations we find in statutes are, for example -- just to give a few examples -- if the second State has a weaker jurisdiction claim, for example, just in nationality of the offender, compared to the stronger basis of the jurisdiction of the State that first prosecuted, for example, territoriality principle, or protective principle, the second State will accept the judgment of the first State as a bar for a second prosecution. Another example: The second State will not waive the exercise of its jurisdiction in case of a previous conviction unless the individual has really served his sentence. Another one: States may bind themselves to deduct the penalty imposed and served abroad from the punishment in which the second trial will result. A last example is that specific procedural safeguards are created in order to prevent that the second prosecution will be started unnecessarily. Since societies became more internationalised and since treaty obligations creating a lot of extra territorial jurisdiction caused the existence of a wide overlap of concurring domestic jurisdiction, a more pressing need was felt to pay tribute to the principle of non bis in idem also at the international level, rather than exclusively at a domestic level. The first and easiest solution to the problem was the expansion of the scope of extradition treaties by granting extradition aiming at the enforcement of a sentence, also for a wide range of offences including sex offence, all kind of other offences that were beyond the scope of extradition treaties before. It became unnecessary to initiate a second prosecution in order to avoid that the individual, that could not be extradited in the early days, would escape justice. The development of the system of transfer of proceedings -- I may refer to the European Convention on the transfer of proceedings in criminal matters that has been produced as an annex of the Prosecutor to the motion on non bis in idem -- resulted in prosecutions in those States where they are likely to be most successful both from the point of view of the Prosecution, availability of witnesses etc., as well as from a point of view of the defendant, avoidance of a second trial. Extraditions aiming at bringing the defendant to trial supported the system of transfer of proceedings, this system which was aiming at the allocation of one single prosecution there where it best met the requirements of criminal justice. As a final step in this development, the transfer of prisoners or the transfer of the enforcement of foreign sentences also diminished the need of a second trial if the individual involved was hiding in a State that could not extradite. Slowly, most of these criminal policy considerations aiming at the concentration of jurisdiction and avoiding double jeopardy found their way into treaty provisions. Non bis in idem chapters have been incorporated in -- I mentioned it already -- the European Convention on the transfer of proceedings, the European Convention on the international validity of criminal judgments and later on even a special Convention on the principle of non bis in idem has been elaborated by what is now the European Union, and it is open for ratification even for not Member States already since 25th May 1987. But let me put a vital question to myself before you do it: Are these developments such that these domestic provisions or treaty provisions I have referred to would bar a second prosecution under the circumstances as we find them in our present case? The answer must be clear, they would not. Apart from the question of the applicability of these provisions, they are not applicable, as we can agree with the Prosecution, the present case would not meet the requirements. If the Tribunal were just an ordinary court of a second State, and just, for argument sake, assuming that the State had a basis for jurisdiction, if that State wanted to prosecute Mr. Tadic for a second time, many reasons would make a defence on a non bis in idem principle fail. I will just give you two: The first one is that there is no final judgment, either a conviction or an acquittal. The second, even if there would have been a conviction, the sentence had not yet been fully enforced. As you may have noticed, I make no reference to the strength of the jurisdictional basis of the previous prosecution. I will come to that later. Of course, I hasten to add to what I have just said, that the situation is different, you are not an ordinary court, we are not a second country. We have to rely on the Statute of this Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is, however, useful to keep in mind the development of the non bis in idem rule under the domestic law and in the law of treaties prior to this new era of the Tribunal. It has been stressed again and again that the Tribunal finds itself in a unique position. This also enables the Defence to develop the non bis in idem argument on the very basis of its rationale and, of course, against the background of the Statute and the Rules of Procedure, but not on the basis of the existing domestic treaty law, but analysing the provisions of the Statute of the Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. A vital part of my argument will be the interrelation between Articles 9 and 10 of the Statute. So let me start there. Article 9 of the Statute -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you one moment? When you get to that portion of your argument, would you then be arguing non bis in idem or are you talking about primacy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would try to explain to you that, first of all, the two are interrelated. The interrelationship between Articles 9 and 10 of the Statute will be explained by me. Then I will say there is a violation of the procedural aspect of non bis in idem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Make sure you make the connection because you have filed a motion on primacy and at least that was part of the motion on jurisdiction. We have heard that, of course. Then there was an appeal and the Appeals Chamber has dealt with, of course, certain issues on primacy. Your points (4) and (5), I think, in your motion which you are now proceeding to, it seemed to me, to be a reargument of primacy but cast in a new way. I just want you to know what I am thinking. I may be totally wrong, but that is what I am thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I will pay some attention to the decision of the Appeals Chamber. The difference, in my view, is at that moment we were arguing that a Tribunal with a primary jurisdiction could not have been created. What I am dealing with today is the way the Articles 9 and 10 have been used in this specific case. So, I am not arguing that primacy as such is not acceptable, but that the way the deferral procedure was used in this case includes a violation of the non bis in idem principle, as we find it, in the Statute, according to my analysis. So, I see the relation but I hope to be able to convince you that it is not entirely the same matter, because I do understand that you are not very much inclined to serve as a second Appeals Chamber above the other Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Also that second argument that you are now proceeding to, I looked at your brief that you filed with the Appeals Chamber -- I looked at it yesterday -- and you raised it in a very kind of -- it was not that clear, but it seems to me you did raise it. I do not know whether it has been addressed by the Appeals Chamber. I have not looked at the transcript and I was not here, so I do not know whether you argued it before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will refer to the decision of the Appeals Chamber. As I said already when we started, if there might be some unclear parts of the motion, this was due to the fact that we were still struggling at that time with quite many problems. I hope to be clear at least today. I will just express that a vital part of argument will be the interrelation between the Articles 9 and 10 of the Statute and that is where I will start. Article 9 of the Statute deals with concurrent jurisdiction and Article 10 of the Statute deals with non bis in idem. What does this mean, concurrent jurisdiction? It is the opposite of exclusive jurisdiction. Both the Tribunal and the domestic courts may have competence to try the relevant offences. States even are encouraged to exercise jurisdiction. As the Secretary-General writes in his Report in paragraph 64, I quote: "In establishing an International Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, it was not the intention of the Security Council to preclude or prevent the exercise of jurisdiction by national courts with respect to sufficient acts. Indeed, national courts should be encouraged to exercise their jurisdiction in accordance with their relevant national laws and procedures." Being the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and States concurrent, the question of the solution of the positive jurisdiction conflict arises. An explicit answer to that question is given in Article 10, in case one of the jurisdictions has resulted in a final judgment. If a procedure is still pending in a national court, Article 9, section 2, provides the possibility of a deferral. The criteria for exercising primary jurisdiction are not explicitly mentioned in Article 9 of the Statute. They are, however, in Article 10, section 2, of the Statute. Does this mean that the criteria of Article 10, section 2 -- I will just name them to you -- first, the under qualification of the crimes, second, that the proceedings were not impartial or independent, third, that the proceedings shielding the accused from international criminal responsibility or the, fourth, that the case was not diligently being prosecuted. Does it mean that these criteria of Article 10, section 2, only apply when a case has resulted in a judgment at a domestic level? This was certainly not the intention of the permanent members of the Security Council. I quote the interpretive statements of France, the United States and the United Kingdom on this issue. France emphasised that, "The Tribunal may intervene at any stage of the procedure and assert its primacy including from the stage of investigations where appropriate in the situations covered under Article 10, paragraph 2." The representative of the United States said that, "It is understood that the primacy of the International Tribunal referred to in paragraph 2 of Article 9 only refers to the situations described in Article 10." The United Kingdom stated that the primacy of the Tribunal was to be interpreted as relating, I quote "primarily to the courts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia; elsewhere it will only be in the kind of exceptional circumstances outlined in Article 10, paragraph 2, that primacy should be applicable". Shraga and Zacklin in their Article that has been referred to before write: "Members of the Security Council indicated upon the adoption of Resolution 827 that intervention in legal proceedings before national courts would only be appropriate in situations covered under Article 10, section 2, of the Statute, namely, to guarantee the objectivity and impartiality of national courts when trying persons responsible for crimes under this Statute, and to ensure that judicial proceedings in national courts are not instituted with the sole purpose of obstructing the jurisdiction of the Tribunal or otherwise shielding the accused from international criminal responsibility". As far as the authority of my sources is concerned, my first quotations, I borrowed them, not from the original document, but I borrowed them from Morris and Shaff, the guide, the green guide, to the International Tribunal, I recall that both Virginia Morris and Ralph Zacklin were members of the working group that prepared the Report of the Secretary General. Therefore, they were deeply involved in the history of this Tribunal. What we see then is that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not respect this unanimous interpretation by the majority of the permanent members of the Security Council and, to some extent, they were even supported by a Russian statement. Rule 9 -- we are talking about Article 9 of the Statute -- of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence goes beyond the intention as expressed by France, US and the United Kingdom. Although the criteria of Article 10, section 2, of the Statute are incorporated in Rule 9, an additional criterion is formulated. It says: "What is in issue is closely related to or otherwise involves significant factual or legal questions which may have implications for investigations or prosecutions before the Tribunal". The Defence submits that the extension of the deferral criteria beyond the criteria as set out in Article 10, section 2, of the Statute, is in contradiction with, if not the wording, at least the purpose and the spirit of the Statute, as expressed in the interpretive statements. The adoption of Rule 9 was in this respect beyond the powers of the judges of this Tribunal and, therefore, cannot be applied being contradictory to the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, but if I may interrupt you at this stage to just follow what you are saying? Is not 10(2) concerned with a situation where there has been a trial and it is over, and is not 9(2) concerned with a quite different situation at any stage of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to that later. I will explain to you that, for sure, that is what it says. First, we have the problem of the applicability of the criteria of Article 10 for the situation of Article 9. The second one is whether at any stage would take away from us any sensible defence of non bis in idem. If you allow me, I will not forget it; I will come to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not hear you correctly, but are you saying that France, Britain and the United States and, perhaps, also Russia said that 10(2)(a), (b) are applicable to 9(2)?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said; all the three of them in quite clear wordings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Were they not saying that the Tribunal may by virtue of Article 9 -- were they not saying there is concurrent jurisdiction but that the Tribunal has primacy and that, therefore, because of this primacy they may at any stage of the procedure request a national court to defer? They may ask, but those national courts need not necessarily comply because it is really limited to those situations of where one of those events occurring in 10(2)(a) and (b) occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, it does not say -- perhaps I will read slowly again the parts I quoted again because, in my opinion, they say quite clearly that you can only use your primacy under Article 9 if the criteria set out in Article 10(2) are met.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is where I have a problem, use it. We may ask, if we choose, but should a country decide that they will not defer for whatever reason, then they may be able to get away with it. Of course, that is not what happened here; Germany did defer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, there are two different questions; the first, whether the Tribunal can use its powers under Article 9 even in the situation which is not covered by the criteria of Article 10(2); the second question is if the Tribunal uses its powers, whether a national State could refuse to defer the case. As far as I see, is that Germany (and now I turn to the particular aspects of this case) felt under an obligation without asking any further questions to comply with the request for deferral.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe in part that was because, as I understand it, Mr. Tadic did not object to the deferral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you. If you look at the history of the German legislation, I do not think that it would have made any difference at all because the Germans say: "If the Tribunal ask it, we will have to do it". They might have overlooked this relation between Article 9 and Article 10 because they feel only entitled to test whether the Tribunal is competent to hear the case, the merits of the case, on the basis of Articles 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the Tribunal, so the subject matter jurisdiction. So, it is my feeling that that has not been the important reason why the case was deferred. But my first problem is that the Tribunal requested a deferral. The question of whether Germany could have acted otherwise, denying it, is not one of the questions that is the most important one for my argument at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You were very usefully threatening to read more slowly what was said by the UK and in the US?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The French emphasised that, and I quote, "The Tribunal may intervene at any stage of the procedure and assert its primacy including from the stage of investigations where appropriate in the situations covered under Article 10, paragraph 2". The United States statement was, "It is understood that the primacy of the international Tribunal referred to in paragraph 2 of Article 9 only refers to the situations described in Article 10." The United Kingdom stated that the primacy of the Tribunal was to be interpreted as relating, and now I quote, "primarily to the courts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia; elsewhere it will only be in a kind of exceptional circumstances outlined in Article 10, paragraph 2, that primacy should be applicable". So, it does not say whether the Tribunal has to decide or whether the requested State has to decide. If I may proceed, your Honours? I then gave you the quotation of Shraga and Zacklin. I pointed out that they were highly involved in the history of this Tribunal. I continued that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence did not respect this relation between the Articles 9 and 10 of the Statute. I quoted the third criterion that has been added in Rule 9 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is important to establish that the application for deferral by the Prosecution of October 12th 1994 as well as the formal request for deferral issued by the Tribunal Chamber One at November 8th 1994 are exclusively relying on the third ground, I would say the complementary one, for a deferral request as found in Rule 9 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The first and second ground for deferral in Rule 9 that are consonant to the criteria of Article 10(2) of the Statute have manifestly played no role in the application of the Prosecutor and the formal request for deferral. You well understand, I am not going to dive into the question on whether this criteria (which is not accepted by the Defence) was met or not. I am not going to argue about whether the case of Mr. Tadic was mainly important because it was the first one and, of course, all the first cases will have some consequences for other cases. I am not going to talk about that because my argument is that this new criteria is not -- violates the rules and the spirit of the Statute. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence are intended to provide the necessary details for the effective and efficient functioning of the International Tribunal as envisaged in the Statute. Morris and Shaff write that it is clear that the Rules cannot be contrary to the express language and/or the purpose of the Statute. Article 9(2) of the Statute does not just refer to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but also binds the deferral procedure to the framework of the Statute itself. After having established a link between the criteria of Article 10(2) and Article 9 of the Statute, and that this link has been disregarded in Article 9 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I return to where I started, the classical concept non bis in idem. The Tribunal does not find itself in the classical situation where the rule of non bis in idem applies in an international context.
