This classical situation is characterised by conflicting rather than concurring jurisdiction assumed by two or more equal and sovereign States, all of them entitled to assume jurisdiction in order to protect their national interests. The Tribunal, however, is in a situation where it has to guarantee that the administration of fair justice is guaranteed. It is representing the world community and not serving the interests of national States. To that extent, there is a difference to be observed between the relationship between the Tribunal and the parties to the conflict, on the one side, and the relation between the Tribunal and third parties not involved in the conflict, at the other side. Whenever third States not involved in the conflict exercise their universal jurisdiction over the crimes, be it grave breaches, war crimes or crimes against humanity, they also primarily serve the interests of the world community, not their own national interests. Whenever these third States fulfil their tasks properly, there is no reason for the Tribunal to interfere. The concurring jurisdiction under these circumstances is not a potential conflicting one, but a jurisdiction of that State and of the Tribunal have a common basis. Both the Tribunal and, in this case, the German judiciary were caretakers acting on behalf of the international community. Where conflicting interests between the jurisdiction of the parties involved in the conflict -- these are primarily national interests -- and the jurisdiction of the Tribunal serving the interests of the national community are likely to exist, conflicting interests are likely to be absent between the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and third States. After this analysis of the situation, which provides a satisfactory theoretical explanation for the interpretive statements of the majority of the permanent members of the Security Council, we have to wonder what the consequences should be. Let me first just make a short remark on the relativity of the position I have outlined until now. Third States, even while they are exercising their universal jurisdiction might not always truly serve the interests of the world community on whose behalf they are supposed to have assumed their universal jurisdiction. Loyalty to one of the parties in a conflict might be a reason to disrespect the interests of a fair administration of international justice. On the other hand, one cannot exclude that the exercise of jurisdiction by one of the parties of the conflict, although perhaps aiming mainly at looking after the national interests, nevertheless, entirely fulfil the demands of international justice simultaneously. This implicates that the position of the States exercising their national jurisdiction should never be taken for granted on the basis of the general analysis of the situation. Whether these States were acting upon the supposedly common basis with the Tribunal or on the supposedly conflicting basis should be tested in the particular circumstances by the jurisdiction of the primary nature, and that is the Tribunal. You see, I am not arguing any more that it is not primacy of jurisdiction; it is you who have to decide. When there are no conflicting interests to be served by two of the concurring jurisdictions, we are, as a matter of fact, in a similar position as within a domestic jurisdiction. There will never be a reason to try an individual twice under these circumstances, because the first prosecution is supposed to have sufficiently looked after the interests of the community on whose behalf the jurisdiction was exercised. Therefore, the interest of the individual not to be prosecuted again, even sometimes if new facts have become known, prevails. The Defence has been confronted many times with the approach that the Tribunal is in a unique position which asks for its own solutions. The analysis of the situation in which the Tribunal finds itself in respect of national jurisdiction shows that the non bis in idem rule should find application similarly to the way the principle is functioning in a national context, when, at least, the actual national concurring jurisdiction is properly fulfilling its obligation towards the international community. This is, as I said to you, likely to happen if a third State is exercising its jurisdiction. The rule of non bis in idem can operate, however, as if it was functioning in an international context whenever the national jurisdiction is not properly serving the interests of the international community, which is likely to be the case if one of the parties to the conflict is exercising its jurisdiction. Both the fairness of the trial and the appropriateness of the sanctions, dependent on whether a compatriot or an enemy is prosecuted, are likely to be jeopardised. The analysis I gave is still fully compatible with the interpretive statements. They tell us that the Tribunal primarily serves to avoid both the total lack of prosecution where no State exercises its powers to prosecute, or to interfere where the prosecution is or was unsatisfactory for the reasons stated in Article 10(2) of the Statute. Especially under the latter circumstances, the interests of the international community, the allegation of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law are properly judged in a fair trial, prevail over the interests of the individual not to be repetitiously prosecuted. It is the submission of the Defence that there is no reason to believe that the prosecution of the defendant in Germany met one of the criteria of Article 10(2) of the Statute. The German proceedings were entirely in conformity with the requirements of the international community. It was not a sham prosecution. It was meeting the basic standards of a fair trial. So, there was no justification for the deferral of the case from Germany to the Tribunal under Article 9 interpreted in accordance with Article 10(2) of the Statute resulting in a second prosecution of the defendant.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one question on that. You said because there was no basis in the Statute for a request for a deferral, then the proceedings before the Tribunal constitute a second prosecution, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is a very difficult question because -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have a transcript and we can read it right back, can we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: At least there is no provision that says how to bring the case back to Germany, but while we are confronted now and then with situations where the Rules do not give a proper solutions, but what I am saying -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know why I asked you that question, because does that not presuppose that there was an on-going prosecution in Germany before the deferral?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And that is one point that the Appeals Chamber did decide. They found no prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have not forgotten that problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So I am still trying to get you to link it to non bis in idem, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I will come to that later. One of my problems is that this issue was not particularly discussed when we were talking about the primacy of jurisdiction as a general problem. As you see in my reasoning, I am accepting the primacy of jurisdiction as a principle valid in this Tribunal. I am now dealing with how it was used in this specific case. Then, I am afraid, that -- I will come to that -- the Appeals Chamber has drawn conclusions on issues that were not really in discussion there. I will explain it. They say they were just investigating the case, there was no prosecution. I will come to that more in detail in a few pages. Even if we were to observe the rule of non bis in idem similarly to its application in a national context due to the identical rather than conflicting underlying interests of the exercise of jurisdiction, there still remain a few questions. Is a final judgment necessary to invoke the protection against a second trial? In the international context, whenever a State is inclined to respect a foreign judgment, the answer will be in the affirmative. Treaty provisions dealing with the non bis in idem show this quite clearly. But in the context of national criminal law, the answer is in the negative, however. Let me just, for example, look at the double jeopardy rule in the United States. The bar against double jeopardy applies only after jeopardy has attached, but this does not automatically mean that a verdict will be given. Even staying apart from the situation of a hung jury -- I am not very familiar with the jury system -- a mistrial not granted upon manifest necessity may put the double jeopardy rule in operation. You will find similar provisions in other jurisdictions. There is not always a final judgment needed in order to prevent a second proceeding to be initiated. There is a stage in most domestic procedures that is considered to be a point of no return. This is usually the beginning of the public trial or, at least, a stage where the decision is taken whether or not a public trial is justified or, to stick to my example of the United States, once the jury has been sworn in in a jury trial. Unfortunately, we have no jury trials in Germany so it is a bit difficult to compare. So, it seems that the question of whether this stage has been reached in the German trial -- I am talking about a trial, not about an investigation -- it seems that this question is already answered by the Appeals Chamber in its decision of 22nd September. Although we were then discussing the principle of primacy of jurisdiction and not primarily the specific way the Tribunal deals with the prior German prosecution, the Appeals Chamber learns the Defence that the German proceedings only reached the stage of an investigation. In support, the Appeals Chamber quotes the deferral decision of November 8th 1994. I quote part of the decision of the Appeals Chamber: "The Prosecutor asserts, and it is not disputed by the government of the Federal Republic of Germany nor by the Council for Dusko Tadic, that the said Dusko Tadic is the subject of an investigation instituted by the national court of the Federal Republic of Germany in respect of the matters listed in paragraph 2 hereof." I draw your attention that in quoting the decision of Trial Chamber One, in fact, the Appeals Chamber is mainly quoting the assertion of the Prosecution. Almost as a reprimand, I would say, the Appeals Chamber continues: "There is a distinct difference between an investigation and a trial. The argument of Appellant, based erroneously on the existence of an actual trial in Germany, cannot be heard in support of his challenge to jurisdiction when the matter has not yet passed the stage of investigation." It should be noted, however, that careful reading of the decision of Trial Chamber One of November 8th 1994 demonstrates that the Trial Chamber was just making reference in the quoted part of the decision to the assertions of the Prosecutor at this stage, when the Prosecutor applied for a formal request for deferral. After this application was filed on 12th October 1994, the defendant was indicted on November 3rd by the competent German authority, of which fact the Trial Chamber shows itself to be aware at the time of the decision. But the Appeal's Chamber also seems to forget, unlike, I must say, the Prosecution in their response to our motion on non bis in idem, that the indictment has been subject to judicial screening by the competent court (the 3rd Senate of the Bavarian Supreme court) and that on 13th February 1995 a "Eroffnungsbeschluss" has been taken. Literally translated, it is an "opening decision". What is opened? The final stage, the trial stage or, as the Germans call it, "das Hauptverfahren", (the main procedure). I will just quote -- the original text are in German. I gave copies already to the Prosecution and I offered three copies for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is in German?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I could also just leave them with you. It is just the Rules that are providing for opening the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it your position that jeopardy has attached in Germany?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For support of that you are giving us this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the Prosecutor has made reference already to the decision, and I think the decision is -- I am not quite sure about that -- in the materials that we have discussed before, that this decision is there, but -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All I want to know is, is it your position that jeopardy has attached in Germany with the issuance of the indictment and whatever else happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Upon the indictment that the German court ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Under German law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- had decided that the trial stage was opened.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not what I am asking, though, because the trial stage may be open, but still jeopardy has not attached. I mean, the trial, I suppose, may begin with opening statements, but perhaps until there is evidence offered on guilt, jeopardy may not have attached in my system, for example. What I am asking you is in Germany has jeopardy attached because I gather that is your position or maybe it is not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is my position, but, of course, we have a problem that the criminal procedures in the systems you are familiar with and in Germany might be totally different. In Germany, we have a three-stage procedure. I would say the first part is the investigative part. Even judges may be involved in giving orders for certain procedures, etc. etc. Then there comes a moment where the investigations, at least in the view of all the competent authorities, are completed. Then we have a short stage, an intermediary stage, of the procedure, what the Germans call the "Zwischenunfahren", that is the procedure in between. Then, thirdly, we have the trial stage. What a happens in the intermediate procedure is that all the evidence is presented. The indictment has been served at that moment already upon the defendant. He may take his position towards the indictment,. He may ask for further investigations. There is even power for the court to decide this just on itself. But then the court says: "This material, this evidence, is good enough to start a trial so we decide that the trial will start now."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In Germany, if the indictment had been dismissed for some reason, could Germany -- let us set aside the deferral and everything about this proceeding -- have reindicted and proceeded against Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think it could be in Germany but I am not applying German -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If so, then jeopardy did not attach vis-a-vis Germany now. That is really my question, in setting aside the whole Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is usually, but we are facing a situation which is unique, because once this decision has been taken that the trial is over, it cannot stop until there is a final judgment, but, I am afraid that the special legislation that had to be made because of the request of the Tribunal changed the German procedure a little bit. So, under normal circumstances, it is unthinkable, unlike perhaps in many other systems, that the case will stop without, the case may be postponed, that is what we saw, it might be done a lot of other things, but finally there will be a decision. So the situation will never -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Indictments are dismissed. It is probably the rare case but indictments are filed, motion is filed to dismiss the indictment for a number of reasons. They are dismissed and then they reindict. No jeopardy has attached and they go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in systems you are familiar with but under German law, as far as I understand it, I am not an expert. I have some experience in that country. The trial may be postponed, it may happen, whatever thing, but it can never start again. It can never be opened again. They will continue on the existing trial or they might temporarily stop it, but it is never to start a new trial when the old one has been started already. So, it is a different position, perhaps, from many other systems. What we are facing here is a lot of particular aspects of quite a lot of national systems, but one thing is for sure, if the Appeals Chamber said it was just another investigation, we cannot believe that solely on the basis of the situation that existed at the time that the application was made by the Prosecution that that can be the basis for the final decision. So we came to a point of no return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You say that it is factually wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is factually wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I do not think it is factually wrong because at the time that the application for deferral was filed, it was in the investigation stage. So, when they make that reference they are referring to the time that the application for deferral was filed. At that time there was only investigation. The indictment was issued later and you are correct that the indictment had been issued at the time that Mr. Tadic was transferred to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is for sure. But the reference in the Appeals Chamber is at a time when the request for deferral was made. At that point there was no indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you, but what is said that the Defence arguing that there was a trial is wrong, because in the first stage it was just an investigation. Of course, we have the next question: What is the relevant time? The time of the application? The time of the decision of Trial Chamber One where they made a formal request for deferral, or the time where Germany was deferring the case to the Tribunal? Of course, you will understand that for the defendant that last situation, in what stage was the procedure at the time that the procedure was stopped and he was brought to the Hague, that is for him, the most important .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your argument is (and we are still trying to connect Article 9 and Article 10) that Rule 9(iii), the Rule, our Rules of Procedure, Rule 9(iii), goes beyond Article 9 because Article 9(B) -- I think it is B, at least it is the second paragraph, I guess, is 2, Article 9(2) is limited to situations set out in Article 10(2). So if that is true -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is not of vital importance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It may be important because the question then, if it is your position that the Tribunal may not make an application for a deferral except in situations envisioned under Article 10(2), then what existed at the time that the application was made, it seems to me, is very critical. What existed at that time in Germany was the investigation, not an indictment. You see, that is your connection between the concurrent jurisdiction and non bis in idem, primacy and non bis in idem. I am trying to get you to connect it. But we can set that aside and say that that is not the situation; that what we need to do is to look at the situation today and let us see what we have. What we have is an indictment in Germany and an attempt at this point to go forward with the prosecution after there has been an indictment in Germany, and what is the effect of that? If the issuance of an indictment in Germany results in jeopardy being attached and non bis in idem applies from one jurisdiction to another -- and then you discussed that very well, I mean, typically you say it applies within one jurisdiction, but now we are talking about international principles -- so if it applies, this concept of non bis in idem from one jurisdiction to the Tribunal, then I think it is critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not think it is, but I will try to explain to you. If the reason for the deferral -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have been talking now for an hour. It is very important for us to understand your argument, because when we all go home if we do not understand your argument, it is not going to be to your advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have just two-and-a-half pages left, so it will not take very long. So I gave you the text of the legal provisions in Germany indicating what is the type of the decision taken in the Eroffnungsbeschluss. Such a decision to open the final stage, the trial stage, of the proceedings is taken after the Prosecutor has presented all evidential material, at least in writing, not representing witnesses, after the indictment has been served upon the defendant, and after he has had the opportunity to present challenges to the material presented and to introduce new issues relating to the evidence. The third senate did not use its power to order new investigations, but by deciding to open the trial stage it found the preliminary investigations sufficiently completed. The Defence, therefore, has difficulties in following the Appeals Chamber in its conclusion that the matter -- we discussed this already -- had not yet passed the stage of investigation. That stage, in our opinion, was closed at least at the time of the deferral itself and the new stage was opened, although this might not become apparent from the only source upon which the Appeals Chamber relied. I will come to one of your particular questions that I had in mind already. Does Article 9 of the Statute not however demonstrate that the deferral may be formally requested at any stage of the procedure? Yes, it does. But, as I have argued before, the criteria of Article 10(2) of the Statute should be met. The reason why I am challenging the determination by the Appeals Chamber of the stage the German proceedings had reached is that the advanced stage of the proceedings in Germany even more clearly demonstrate how the deferral infringes upon the right of the defendant not to be subject to a second prosecution when the criteria of Article 10(2) are not met. Here it becomes clear that although I paid some attention to it in order to indicate that the stage of the proceedings might be of some importance in a domestic context, whether or not to allow a second prosecution, my argument was that deferral under Article 9 at any stage of the procedure after the trial had started, before the trial had started, was only possible if the conditions under Article 10(2) had been met. So, as I told you before, it is not of vital importance for my argument, but it is very important to demonstrate what the consequences are for the defendant. That is what I have written down. What is the sense of all this? If the proceedings in a national system have not yet finally reached a trial stage, but were hampering shortly before that stage -- that is a situation almost similar to the situation in which Mr. Tadic finds himself; while not much of the trial actually took place because that is clear, the trial has been opened but since then nothing happened -- in national systems, if it had come near to that point, a second prosecution was possible. So, there would under these almost similar circumstances, just after the beginning of the trial or just before the beginning of the trial, before the beginning of the trial there would be no non bis in idem rule or no double jeopardy rule to be applied. So the question is, what is bothering the Defence if we refer to the national context? If the non bis in idem rule in a domestic context fails to apply because the trial stage has not finally been reached, the defendant -- that is the difference with the domestic situation and a situation where a case is deferred from Germany to the Tribunal -- is far less disadvantaged than he is in the present situation. All the investigative measures remain valid within a domestic context if the proceedings will be resumed in a second trial. I am not talking about a second prosecution but if they start over prosecuting him again. It is not necessary to start all over again the pretrial interrogations of the defendant and of witnesses. That is perhaps the most important difference, that the pretrial detention in such a domestic context will be taken into consideration even where the prosecution will be resumed in a second round after the first proceedings had failed to result in a final judgment, or in a stage where we can say that there was a trial. It is with respect to this last issue that the Tribunal fails to meet proper standards of justice. Rule 101 -- we have discussed it this morning as well -- under E reads: "Credit shall be given to the convicted person for the period, if any, during which the convicted person was detained in custody pending his surrender to the Tribunal or pending trial or appeal". The defendant, Mr. Tadic, has spent approximately 14 months in German detention. Of these 14 months, only a very short period of time, knowingly on and after April 18th 1995, the defendant has been detained in custody pending his surrender to the Tribunal. From that moment, the detention in Germany was serving his deferral to the Tribunal. The Defence submits that the third ground adopted in Rule 9 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence is inconsistent with the Statute. But if such a Rule had to be adopted, and if the deferral proceedings were to function not only in the exceptional circumstances as described in Article 10(2), then at least the Rules of Evidence and Procedure should have reflected the same liberal approach by giving credit as well for the time spent in detention as a result of the exercise of the domestic jurisdiction prior to the request for deferral. These material disadvantages s are the reason why the Defence felt that it had to challenge the legitimacy of a deferral under a criterion that does not find its roots in the Statute and violates its spirit. The result is a violation of the non bis in idem principle in its procedural aspect, being this aspect part of the integral principle that has been incorporate in the Statute in the Articles 9 and 10 together.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just ask a couple of questions of you? The request for deferral was made in February of this year; is that correct? The application, I guess, it is a request for an application for a deferral -- I am pretty sure it was made in February. I do not have the dates before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think the application has been filed by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Filing of the application for a formal request for deferral.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was November of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was 12th October 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: October. The hearing and the decision -- November 8th 1994 was the date of the decision granting the request for a deferral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At that hearing, it is my understanding -- we have talked about this before -- the accused did not oppose deferral, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you not believe then that the accused should be estopped at this point from challenging the appropriateness of the deferral?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think that is a difficult problem. Also, you will see that this problem is dealt with under different systems in different ways. There are systems where you say even if you agree with a procedural act which is not in accordance with the applicable provisions that you can challenge later this procedural act even -- I mean, waiver is not absolute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You cannot waive constitutional rights or something like that. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the theory I am referring to. I must say, without being impolite to one of my German colleagues -- it has been the same situation for us -- I do not know whether they were fully aware of all the consequences. In a normal procedural situation, if you are assisted by counsel, you are supposed to have a clear idea of what the consequences are of the position you take. For example, I do not know whether Mr. Tadic was aware of all the investigations have to start all over again, but Mr. Wladimiroff was more involved in that stage of the procedure so I would like to -----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I was not involved, but I should point out that the German lawyer acted not as a counsel for Mr. Tadic at the deferral proceedings, he was admitted as amicus curiae. So, for that reason I think the statement of Mr. Sklebitz is not binding to the extent that it could block Mr. Tadic to take the position as he does now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of other questions. Article 10 of the Tribunal Statute provides that a person who has been tried -- tried -- by a national court for acts constituting serious violations of international humanitarian law may be subsequently tried by the International Tribunal only if (a) the act for which he or he she was tried was characterised as an ordinary crime, or (b) the national court proceedings were not impartial or independent, were designed to shield the accused from international criminal responsibility, or the case was not diligently prosecuted. So, saying that, this Article provides that a person who has been tried by a national court may only be tried by the Tribunal under these circumstances. OK. It is your position, I gather, then that Mr. Tadic has been "tried", no? OK. Then what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have not made myself clear. What I tried to explain -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As it relates to non bis in idem, we will get to the primacy argument in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is I am not bound by the heading non bis in idem in Article 10. I am making a distinction between the procedural aspect, and the concurrent jurisdiction has something to do with the procedural aspect of non bis in idem. There is a relation. It is not without reasons that in the Report of the Secretary general both the paragraphs are dealt with in a one single commencement. There is a link. What I say is not that he has been tried finally in Germany, but that under Article 9 a deferral procedure, that means that not at the end of the procedure the case will be brought to the Tribunal, but already pending investigation or trial, that the case is deferred to the Tribunal, so, before a final decision has been taken, that the same criteria that are explicitly mentioned in Article 10 for the situation where there is a judgment do apply under Article 9. That is what I learn from the interpretive statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is your primacy argument. Your primacy argument it seems -- let Judge Stephen. You repeat it because your primacy argument, as I see it, is that Article 9 provides that the International Tribunal shall have primacy over national courts. It then provides that at any stage of the proceedings the International Tribunal may formally request national courts to defer to the competence of the International Tribunal in accordance with the present Statute and Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal. What you say is, look to what Mme. Albright says, look to what the French representatives said. What they said is that Article 9(2), that is, the deferral, is limited to situations where in the national courts they are considering a situation that exists on under 10(2), right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. That is a primacy argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Not, it is not, in my opinion. I will try to explain to you why.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I think that is a primacy argument because, what you are saying, if you fail to abide by that, and then this is the connection to the non bis in idem, then what you are doing is trying the accused twice. Is that the non bis in idem component of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Why it is not the primacy argument, we discussed in a prior stage of this proceedings the principle of primacy of this Tribunal over national jurisdictions. I accept that there is primacy. This means, in my opinion, that it is the Tribunal that decides on whether the criteria of Article 10 are met or not. It is not the State, it is the Tribunal that can say: "We are in a situation where the Statute gives us the opportunity, gives us in general terms the primacy. So, it is us who decide the issue, and then we look at the Statute and we see that the requirements necessary in order to use our primacy situation, to use the primacy of jurisdiction, are met so we are doing it."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When may we use this primacy jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When may we use this primacy jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If the criteria of Article 10 ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In 10(2) are met?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So what are you saying then again is: "Yes, there is concurrent jurisdiction, yes, there is primacy jurisdiction, but the Tribunal may only use this primacy jurisdiction when the act for which he is tried is characterised as an ordinary crime or that the national court proceedings are impartial or independent".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then I came back to the basics of the non bis in idem principle.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So that is the primacy argument. How does then the action of this Tribunal in requesting a deferral and having the deferral accepted by Germany not opposed, how does that then violate the non bis in idem principle?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I have given an analysis of the non bis in idem principle, not only as the term is used in Article 10.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I talked about a procedural aspect and about the aspect of not being punished. So this means that if you go on with the procedure almost to the end and say: "OK, we start it all over again", then this is a violation of the procedural aspect of the non bis in idem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So then what you are saying then is that, first of all, the primacy is limited to those situations and in this situation it is a violation of non bis in idem because of what transpired in Germany?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Both because the requirements were not met and, apart from that, that the procedure in Germany reached already an advanced stage, so that the reasons for the defendant to oppose against the deferral are even stronger than if this could have been, let us say, one week after having been arrested in Germany when the whole case could have been dealt with -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then it seems to me that we look at the situation at the time of the deferral. As I understand it, at the time of the decision of the deferral there was only an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what you take for the time of the decision of the deferral.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, for example, the decision in Germany that the case would defer to the Tribunal was from -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: November 1994, the Tribunal issued a request for deferral. At that time no indictment had been issued. There was not -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The indictment had been issued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In November?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: 3rd November, the indictment had been issued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have the date of the decision of deferral.

utterances.speaker: MISS FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: It was the 8th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. So then the decision on the deferral was made after the indictment had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Hague decision. Then upon the request the Germans still had to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So, we have the application, then the decision taken in the Hague. The request for deferral could not be complied with by the Germans because there was no legislation at all. So, finally, the decision on the deferral was only taken after the opening of the trial stage and that was in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Even if the Tribunal's authority to request deferral was not limited to the situations of 10(2)(a) and (b) as you assert, even if that were not the case, it would still be your position that the decision on the deferral having come after the issuance of an indictment by Germany would constitute a violation of non bis in idem, not as phrased in our Statute, but the general recognised right to not be tried twice, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not the situation, so I am happy that at least I have a stronger argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except that I still am having a problem with your link between primacy, what I consider to be primacy, which is another challenge to primacy, which is a significant issue, because the members of the Security Council talked about this, and they talked about what is the meaning of Article 9. As you said, many of them said: "Look, countries must comply but only in the situation set forth in 10(2)", yet our rules in 9(iii) provide for a much broader right of deferral. The question may be that that is simply a request for deferral and we have interpreted that to mean as 9(2) says, at any stage of the proceeding we may ask. But should the country say; "Look, my representative at the Security Council, before any of this began, interpreted it this way; we are not going to comply because it does not meet 10(2)". That is a possibility, and that is why it is an important issue that you have raised. You did raise that a little bit before the Appeals Chamber in your brief on page 6 where you say that "even if the case against the accused was diligently prosecuted, domestic proceedings were impartial and independent and were not designed to shield the accused from international, criminal responsibility", you were then challenging -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We touched upon the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But it was not dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was not dealt with, at least it was not our intention to deal with it to the full extent. What we see now, and what I am arguing now, is that we accept the primacy. This means for us that we accept that the Tribunal decides whether there will be a request for a deferral, whether under the circumstances of Article 10(2) states have the obligation to co-operate, etc. These are all consequences of the primacy. That is what we have to respect after the decision of the Appeals Chamber. Now we come down to a different issue, that is, when we respect the primacy of the Tribunal, this does not mean that we respect the way this primacy is used under every circumstance, and then we rely upon our interpretation of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I am saying to you is that even if we did not even look at Article 10, the argument you have presented today is that he was indicted, Mr. Tadic was indicted ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- and at that point any further proceedings by this Tribunal pursuant to a deferral would violate his right not to be tried again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That would be our main argument. Now it is just an illustration because, as a first argument, we rely upon the inconsistency between Rule 9 and the Statute. But if there would not have been such a conflict between Rule 9 and Articles 9 and 10 of the Statute, then that would be our main argument to rely upon. So it is now just an additional argument.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we need resolve this question? Do we need to at this point make the decision as to whether or not our Rule 9(iii) violates the Statute in that Article 9(2) is limited to situations envisioned under Article 10(2)? Is that something we need to resolve today to deal with your double jeopardy argument, non bis in idem argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you will have to decide upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that, apart from the interpretive remarks of the members of the Security Council to which you have drawn attention, apart from that, there would be no reason other than to give the literal interpretation to Article 9(2) at any stage of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps because I had in mind that such a question could be asked of me, I paid a lot of attention to why these interpretive remarks are logical, legally logical, when we think at the basic aspects of the functioning of the rule of non bis in idem in the international or in the internal context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course, if you call it autre fois acquit or autre fois convict, it loses all that significance because there was no conviction, there was no acquittal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is why I made it quite clear that if we look at the treaties, if you look at quite a lot of domestic provisions, the answer will be that there is no non bis in idem defence. But I tried to elaborate the problem and the issue in the specific circumstances of the Tribunal facing another country that exercised already to a large extent its universal jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The only prejudice, really, which you invoke is the interpretation of "pending" as not merely before but before and awaiting surrender?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite clear that it has been decided in Germany only after the new legislation had been enacted that the detention of Mr. Tadic was based upon the warrant of arrest issued by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think it is a very harsh interpretation when one comes to sentencing that one ignores the previous incarceration which preceded but was not in the light of the surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at Rule 101 you see that when, I would say, national detention is mentioned it just says ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It just says "custody" and the question is whether the accused was in custody because of a request on the part of the Tribunal to detain him, or whether he was in custody because of the Germany authorities’ investigation. What you have said is that it appears that that Rule only gives us the right to give credit at the time served from the time he was in custody as a result of Tribunal's request which may be harsh but ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: He was not incarcerated waiting the deferral to the Tribunal, but he was incarcerated because he was under warrant of arrest under German law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It depends upon the meaning of "pending" and you are probably right, but I would be sorry if you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather be careful in this respect and not to take it for granted that you interpret all the rules according to our expectations.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions as it related to your motion that you filed. You have five points. First you say "prosecution in Germany". In that motion, and because it is a little bit different than your argument today, your argument today really went off on non-bis-in-idem, primacy and the connection, but let me see if I can get an idea of your position based on the paper that you filed. Your first point was the prosecution in Germany. You said that the trial has already been started in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That of course you say would violate the general proposition of non-bis-in-idem; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read -- you are referring to what part of the motion at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Point one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the present situation has been described under German law, that he was indicted and a trial date had been set, the trial was open.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Point one says: "Prosecution in Germany". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is your position,, I gather, that the trial has already been started in Germany. Is that your position in that point one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather then it would be your position that jeopardy has attached; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, any additional trial before this Tribunal would violate non bis in idem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then in point two you say, "Transferral of criminal case". In that section you have mentioned, and you alluded to it only once today, that Mr. Tadic was not transferred in accordance with the European Treaty. Is that correct, or am I reading the European Treaty on the Transferral of Criminal Prosecution of 1972?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is correct, but as you might have noticed I have given the whole issue a few more, and to some extent some new thoughts as well. I am aware of that and I apologise for that. As I stated before, these treaties as such are not applicable, but of course they help us in understanding the mechanisms of preventing new trials. I do not rely upon the direct applicability of these treaties. I also have been quite clear on the issue that under these treaties and the non-bis-in-idem provisions of these treaties, we would have no non-bis-in-idem defence, because there is no final judgment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As to that point then, the Tribunal clearly not bound by the Treaty, and to the extent that we have obligations that flow from chapter 7 of the Charter, there would be our responsibility to meet that; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not think I understand the point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us not rehash the legality of the establishment of the Tribunal, but in any case we are not bound by that Treaty; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You are not bound by the Treaty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the third point in your motion is called "Separate Prosecution"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, separate prosecution. That is a very different issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a separate prosecution from the earlier one in Germany or is it a continuation of the earlier prosecution? If you look at how the Germans looked at this problem, they thought of a kind of unity between the prosecution started in Germany and the prosecution to be continued in The Hague. I do not know why they thought it, because one of the consequences would have been that not everything had to be done anew and perhaps that pretrial detention would automatically be part of that one united procedure. That is theoretically a very difficult problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am just trying to understand. Were you saying in this motion in point three that the proceeding before the Tribunal is a separate prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unlike the Germans thought.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Germans thought it would be a continuation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That the prosecution here would be a continuation, but in fact this is a separate prosecution; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then in point four that is entitled as "Interpretation of Article 9 of the Statute". That is when you then say that Article 9 of the Statute should be limited to situations described in Article 10(2) of the Statute, and our Rule under Rule 9(iii) which allows for a request for a deferral other than, in cases other than, when the proceeding in the national court is a sham, etc., as provided in 10(2), that is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is not in conformity with the Statute. It is even violating the Statute as interpreted according to the interpretive statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then our Rules then go beyond, Rule 9(iii), the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then finally in point five you say "The Application of Concurrent Jurisdiction". This is when I suppose you are saying that the way that the concurrent jurisdiction provisions of Article 9 were applied by this Tribunal, that this violates the non bis in idem rule. Is in this what you are saying? You say: "The last Article only provides for two cases in which the non bis in idem rule does not apply." I am just reading from your motion. You say: "The manner in which the Tribunal has applied the concurrent jurisdiction Rule of Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Statute, constitutes a breach of the non bis in idem rule of Article 10, paragraph 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we think of the non bis in idem covered in both Article 9 and Article 10 of the Statute, we are not very happy with the wordings of it because the procedural aspect of the non bis in idem appears already in Article 9 section (2) of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So are you saying that the concurrent jurisdiction of Article 9 paragraph 2 of the Statute constitutes breach of the non bis in idem Rule of Article 10 paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is because of the stage the proceedings have reached in Germany. So the first argument is that in whatever State it would be a violation, because the criteria of Article 10, section 2, are not met. The second position is that if they would not be applicable, then at least the stage the procedure has reached in Germany makes it a violation of the non bis in idem Rule to defer the case in that advanced stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who will argue now for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, we have a fourth statement to make on the part of the Defence done by Mr. Vujin. I think he should address the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This relates to the non bis in idem motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I thought you had concluded your argument. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) Concerning the case of the accused Tadic, the principle of non bis in idem, as we see through the provisions of Article 9 and linked to Article 10 of the Statute, or else under Rules 12 and 13 of the Rules on Procedures and Evidence, it is year to us that the Trial Chamber can refuse a motion about that. But the question we should raise is up until when the Defence can put the motion of non bis in idem. This is why we can find ourselves in a situation whereby through concurrent trials in national jurisdictions the accused Tadic could have proceedings brought against him in one of the republics of the Former Yugoslavia, for example, Republica Srpske. Who is the one who should judge whether in these proceedings, which can end by a final sentence, who is going to determine whether the proceedings were impartial and independent? You are going to be in a situation if we present a decision of the court and then file the motion of non bis in idem, in that case you should decide about something else. I would like, therefore, because I have got some indications about that, the Trial Chamber to rule up until when we can file non bis in idem motions. It is clear that we have not got an enforceable decision where non bis in idem can be applied, but we could have it because there might be proceedings against Mr. Tadic which this Trial Chamber ignores.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Statute passed by Germany I understand specifically provides that he may not be retried -- I do not have it before me but I have looked at it and that Statute ----

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) It is not a problem about Germany legislation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That Statute provides that regarding the law regulating the co-operation with the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, that Statute provides that criminal proceedings may no longer be conducted against a person against whom the Tribunal has taken or is taking action. That is Germany. As to other countries, we also have an Article in our Statute, the Tribunal Statute, that says that no person shall be tried before a national court for acts constituting serious violations of International Humanitarian Law under the present Statute 4 for which he or she has already been tried by the International Tribunal. So we have a law that deals with the particular circumstances in Germany and then we have our Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) Not for which he is tried. This is not non bis in idem in that case, but something he had already been tried for. Which is the Rule you are referring to now, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was referring to Article 10(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) Yes, but not already been tried which means that a decision, a legal enforceable decision, had already been passed, sentenced. To give you an example, today we have been discussing about the possibility of trial and the possibility to start this trial in March or May. What is going to happen if we, the Defence, give you a fully enforceable sentence about conviction or acquittal of Republica Srpska about Mr. Tadic for crimes, war crimes? Who is going to ask and who is going to verify that the trial had been impartial and independent, that the proceedings had been done in a correct way, and who is going to say that the decision had not been good because it is ended by an acquittal? Who is going to characterise this as an ordinary crime? What if the court said that he is acquitted, he is not guilty? Can we as a defence file the same motion in front of this Trial Chamber? How are you going to react because this has not been regulated?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 10(2) -- let us suppose that Mr. Tadic is tried in absentia by some country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) It is possible in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. Then at that point you then present us with that judgment and the question becomes, as I understand, your question, whether this Tribunal then could go forward with the present trial. What Article 10 says of the Statute is that a person who has been tried by national courts for acts constituting serious violations of international humanitarian law may be subsequently tried by the International Tribunal, only if (a) the act for which he was tried was characterised as an ordinary crime or (b) national court proceedings were not impartial or independent, etc. It would be up to the Tribunal to make that determination. I accept probably what you are feeling and thinking and perhaps even saying that that is a very difficult decision to be made, but that is a decision, it will be just one of many difficult decisions that we have made thus far and may have to make in the future. I do not know that that really impacts on where we are now. I have been trying my best to see what it is that has been decided already by the Appeals Chamber to try to separate primacy from non bis in idem. Perhaps we have been successful. I understand your concern, but I would rather us not look into the future to worry about what will happen. I accept what you say, that if that occurs it will be something that we will have to resolve and it will be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) These are not concerns and it is not a question of difficulties. Every judgment you have to make is difficult; every decision is difficult. This is a question of procedure. The principle of non bis in idem presumes that there is already a sentence, a decision made by a court, and who is going to start the proceedings? The person is judged parallely in front of the other court. Who is going to say that that particular sentence is not valid? This is never set in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What you are suggesting is that 10(2) itself violates the proposition of non bis in idem, that there should not be a provision ----

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) Non bis in idem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- for the Tribunal under any circumstances to try someone who has been tried by a national court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (original: Serbian) That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That has not been raised by the motion and factually it is not really before us. So I understand your concern, but it is not something that is before us today. It is a legitimate concern. We will need to stand in recess for 15 minutes and then when we return we will hear from the Prosecution in response to the non bis in idem motion filed by the Defence. (Short Adjournment) (4.45 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you will be presenting an argument for the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes ma'am. Thank you. If it pleases the court. Once again, your Honours, as in this morning we have a blending or a confusion of issues by the Defence in what was a very creative argument. But that argument aside, we do have the requirements in the standard set forth in our Statute and in our Rules. Article 9 and Article 10 are separate articles and address distinct issues. As opposed to the Defence characterisation of Article 10 modifying Article 9, if you will, in fact we believe more appropriately that Article 10 is a subset of Article 9. Article 9 sets forth the nature of jurisdiction both in the first paragraph concurrent and in 9(2) the primacy of the Tribunal. It says that the Tribunal shall have primacy over national courts, and that in any stage of the procedure the Tribunal may formally request national courts to defer competence. Then in Article 10 what we see, that if you will, is a limitation in the sense of non bis in idem, and is where there has been a final determination by a national court, either a conviction or acquittal, the Tribunal cannot try an accused except in the circumstances set forth therein. We see those as distinct issues. The issue of non bis in idem, which was the motion brought before this Tribunal, as it relates to this Tribunal must be determined in accordance with Article 10 of the Statute, specifically Article 10, subsection (2) for the purposes of cases brought before this Tribunal. The principle requirement for the application of this Rule, as the Defence correctly asserted, is that the accused must have already been tried and a final judgment rendered by a national court. That is not the situation in this case again, as admitted by the Defence. As stated by the Appeals Chamber, this is not an instance of the accused being tried anew by this International Tribunal under the exceptional circumstances described in Article 10 of the Statute. The Prosecution has never sought to bring an appellant before the International Tribunal for a new trial for the reason that one or the other of the conditions enumerated in Article 10 would have vitiated this trial in Germany. Deferral proceedings against the appellant were requested in accordance with the procedure set down in Rule 9 subsection (iii). I understand the Defence's position as regards the German proceedings. However, you have in the materials that were submitted with the Prosecution response both the Act of the Supreme Court of State of Bayern in Germany which was in fact the court that had cognizance over the Tadic case there, both in its original German and the translated version, as well as the German ICTY law and its translated versions, both of which indicate in the first instance and as regards the case of Mr. Tadic that in fact proceedings had never officially opened. The indictment had been accepted by the court. Those proceedings had then been deferred pending the passage of German law. So in fact proceedings never officially opened in the sense of the case starting. The second instance of the German law, as opposed to the characterisation by the Defence that the law simply was, if you will, Germany acting under the coercion of the International Tribunal, instead it actually said, mindful of its obligations to the International Tribunal as set forth in the Security Council resolutions which it cites, it passed its law so that it could defer jurisdiction, which it willingly did, as you hit on earlier in your questions to the Defence ma’am. We have an issue here which is one of a voluntary transfer; not the situation of a forcible imposition of the primacy of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, let me ask you a question, if I may, regarding your first point, that the proceedings in Germany never officially opened. I was trying in my questions to Mr. Orie to get an understanding of the proceedings. Of course we do know there was an investigation and the Appeals Chamber said that there was. But there was also an indictment issued. My question really was designed to determine what does that mean? Does this mean a trial? Does this mean the trial has commenced, or does this mean whatever has happened is sufficient to trigger this right not to be subject to a violation of the non-bis-in-idem principle? You say that they have found that the proceedings never officially opened. Where do I find support for that and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: First off, ma'am, let me say I am not an expert in German law. I am only going by the plain language of the translation of the official German indictments which are submitted. Second of all, I think the standard of Article 10 is very clear. Even if the proceedings had opened, let us say, assuming they had opened, the requirement as a final judgment, I do not believe there has been any evidence or any issue presented by other either party, by the Defence, in fact I believe they agreed that there was no final judgment in Germany, so that is the standard for Article 10. If that has not been reached, then Article 10 does not apply.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know if the Defence agree that the standard is no final judgment. When I asked them about 10(2), a person who has been tried by a national court, the Defence seems to interpret "tried" as meaning something different than a prosecution that results in a verdict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I understand the Defence's argument. I am asserting that the plain language of the Statute is very clear, and it does not leave room for that type of creative interpretation. It says "tried" and in conjunction with the other standard which is present throughout our Statute, that is that the law applicable by the Tribunal must be beyond any question part of International Humanitarian Law, it is clear that the international standard for non bis in idem is a final judgment, both as recognised by the International Covenant for Civil and Political Rights and in fact I believe as agreed by the Defence in their argument most of the other international agreements. In fact, as asserted in our brief, the International Covenant does not have any transnational effect. There is, if you will, no international standard requiring the application of non bis in idem in the international sense, in the transnational sense.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: From one jurisdiction to another?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct. So the fact this Tribunal has chosen, that the Statute obligates this Tribunal to abide by that principle, it then sets forth very clearly what that principle is and it requires a final judgment, period. I do not believe there is any other room for an other interpretation of that language. If Article 10, as we submit, does not apply in this case, period, the issue then becomes of course what are we left with? We would assert that is the issue of the motion and on that basis alone the motion fails, but if we were to get into this issue of the primacy and the relationship between the Rules and the Article -- as the Defence pointed out, paragraph 65 of the Report of the Secretary-General states that the details of how the primacy of the Tribunal will be asserted shall be set out in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So clearly the intent was to give this Tribunal the authority to determine the circumstances of when primacy and how primacy should be asserted. Article 9(2) of the Statute reflects this position wherein it also states: At any stage of the proceedings the Tribunal may request deferral in accordance with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Defence I believe also correctly asserts that in promulgating those rules, of course, the Tribunal cannot exceed the authority granted to it as described and intended by the Statute. The Judges are free, of course, to interpret the Statute and its intent and, in accordance with that intent, adopt its rules. In the context of Article 9 it is clear that the intent of the Security Council was to give the Tribunal primacy over all nations in order to prevent any derogation of the effective administration of justice in these matters by the Tribunal, that might be caused by the effects of any particular nations legal actions against an accused. In adopting Article 9 the Security Council gave the Judges the latitude to determine the appropriate circumstances for deferral within that intent. Article 9(2) does not specifically limit instances of deferral to the circumstances set forth in Article 10(2). The Defence is incorrect in its assertion that Rule 9 subparagraph (iii) is inconsistent with the Statute. It is in fact entirely consistent with the intent of the Statute regarding primacy of the Tribunal. Just as a national trial of an accused conducted under the kinds of circumstances set forth in Article 10(2) could thwart the purpose of the Tribunal, so too could a national investigation or other ongoing criminal proceeding, whether inadvertently or intentionally, because of the issues involved or the way and manner in which the investigation or proceedings were being conducted. If the actions of any nation in the conduct of investigation or adjudication of crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal could thereby impede the full and fair administration of justice by the Tribunal, the Tribunal should be able to assert its primacy. The derogatory effect is no less when the acts of a State are affected by a completed trial or an incomplete investigation or other proceeding. The import of both Article 9 and Rule 9 is to allow the Tribunal to accomplish its purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you look at the Report of the Secretary-General that accompanies Article 9, it simply refers to the Tribunal being permitted to request deferral. It does not say anything about what States may do in compliance, or how States should comply. In paragraph 65 of the Report it says that: "This concurrent jurisdiction, however, should be subject to the primacy of the International Tribunal. At any stage of the procedure the International Tribunal may formally request the national courts to defer to the competence of the International Tribunal." That is tracking right from the Statute in Article 9. "The details of how the primacy will be asserted shall be set out in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal." Then it goes on to say that: "According to principle of non-bis-in-idem, a person shall not be tried twice for the same crime. In the present context, given the primacy of the International Tribunal, the principle of non-bis-in-idem would preclude subsequent trial before a national court. However, the principle of non-bis-in-idem should not preclude a subsequent trial before the International Tribunal in the following circumstances", and then what are set out are the circumstances in 10(2). I suppose the reason I mention that is that we have the comments of various States that Mr. Orie mentioned. How do you interpret those statements? Do you interpret those statements as saying that a request for deferral is not to be made except in circumstances contemplated by 10(2), or do you interpret those statements as saying they may be made as Judge Stephen had asked, as required by 9(2), at any stage of the procedure? However, the states may act on those requests, I suppose, as they choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next point I was going to move to was those comments. If we look at the actual language of 9(2), it says that: "At any stage of the procedure the International Tribunal may formally request national courts". In fact the decision of Trial Chamber One in its decision on the deferral in this case, that is its actual action. If you look at the decision it says: "We formally request the Republic of Germany to defer its proceedings."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At that stage we have learned an indictment had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe that that request can be made consistent with the Rule at any stage of the proceedings. The issue becomes, just as you mentioned, - and that is why I said I believe you hit the issue - is whether you are talking about a voluntary transfer which we have in this case, or what would happen if a national authority said, "No, we do not want to defer because under this issue of concurrence we would rather prosecute in this particular case." What our Statute provides for is that we would then have to go to the Security Council to request sanctions in order to assert, if you will, affirmatively our jurisdiction to try to force that nation to turn over the case. That would be the only avenue of approach to us. I believe it is in that context that we must look at the comments. Again, for example, if we pick the comments of the representative of France. It is page 11 of the document. I am reading from the Security Council resolution. "Thirdly, we believe that pursuant to Article 9, paragraph 2, the Tribunal may intervene at any stage of the procedure and assert its primacy, including from the stage of investigation, where appropriate, in the situations covered under Article 10 paragraph 2." The other comments essentially mirror that. It is the position of the Prosecutor that what those three members of the Security Council were referring to was that in the situation where there was an attempt by the Tribunal to affirmtively assert its authority, they would only impose sanctions in those limited circumstances, where you had one of the circumstances that are also laid out in 10(2), as opposed to the separate issue of the plain language of the Statute which they all voted for which says: "This Tribunal may formally request deferral at any stage of the proceedings". So I think those comments must be read with the full effect of their language, which is the assertion of primacy as opposed to "may request deferral at any stage". So I think that is the context in which those comments were being made, that those Members of the Security Council, those three, felt that they would only, if you will, vote for an affirmative assertion of jurisdiction, that is through sanctions, in those limited circumstances. But that is the enforcement issue and not the question of what does the language of Article 9 mean. That we argue is clear on its face. So those comments are not germane to this case because, as you rightly stated, in this case we had a voluntary transfer by Germany. That is indicated by the decision of the court in Bayern and it is also indicated by the language of the German law for co-operation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Except Mr. Orie would say that the German authorities felt somehow compelled to respond to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I cannot speak for what was on their mind. I can only speak as to what the language of the law reads. I certainly believe that the German authorities were competent to understand their obligations in what they were required and not to required to do under international law. But that still does not face the issue of what does Article 9 say on its face, what occurred in this case, which is there was a voluntary transfer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, in your opinion then does a request for a deferral in a situation other than what is set out in 10(2) of the Statute, is that permitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe Article 10(2) has no relation to a deferral request. Article 10(2) relates only to the issue of a trial before this Tribunal in a case where a final determination has been made by a national court. That is what Article 10, and Article 10(2) specifically, states on its face. That is the circumstance it is limited to. Again, we believe Article 10 is a subset, if you will, of Article 9, discussing only the limited issue of trials here where there has been a final determination in a national court. That is all Article 10 is relevant to, which is again not what we have here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But Mr. Orie would say, at least this is my interpretation of what he said, the principle of non-bis-in-idem would be violated if a request is made for deferral in any situation other than one envisioned by 10(2). I may be mischaracterising his position, but that is certainly what I understood it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As I understood his position ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe not. Maybe I misunderstood. You tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I understood his position to be that he believes that the traditional standards of non bis in idem should not be applied here. I believe his first statement was that the standard interpretation of non bis in idem is exactly what is stated in Article 10.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And in the International Covenant. He is arguing for a more aggressive approach than non bis in idem.
